study protocol description: RNA was isolated from mouse tumor tissue. Tumor chunks of 1 to 2mm in diameter were placed in TRIzol (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA) and homogenized using a Tissue Lyser II (Qiagen, Valencia, CA). Tissue with TRIzol was centrifuged at 1200g and 0.2ml of chloroform was added for 5min. Samples were centrifuged at 10,000g for 15min at 4C. The aqueous phase with RNA was transferred to a 1.5ml eppendorf tube. Isopropyl alcohol (0.5ml) was added to each sample (room temperature) for 10min and samples were centrifuged at 10,000g for 10min at 4C. RNA pellets were washed once with 75% ethanol and resuspended in 100l RNase-free water. Quality and quantity of RNA were measured by an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, Inc., Santa Clara, CA).
Total RNA of 500ng per sample was amplified using Ambion TotalPrep (Ambion), and 1.5g of the product was loaded onto the chips.
Following hybridization at 55C, the chips were washed.
The data was checked with GenomeStudio (Illumina) for quality control. In GenomeStudio, data was background subtracted and rank invariant normalization was applied.
Standard Illumina scanning protocol using Illumina iScan.

Twenty C57BL/6 male mice (Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, ME), having an average lifespan of 878 days (36) were obtained at age 130 days, and another 20 mice were obtained at age 540 days from the National Institute on Aging Rodent Colony before transport to Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL, Upton, NY). The scaling of mouse age to human age was based on published criteria (37). Age comparisons are as follows: mice 143 and 551 days at tumor injection are considered equivalent to 23- and 58-year-old humans. Ten young and 10 middle-aged mice were irradiated for five consecutive days with 0.2 Gy of 56Fe ions (1 GeV/amu) with an LET of 151 keV/lm at BNL. The mice were given whole-body irradiation with the body axis oriented perpendicular to the beam. An additional 10 young and 10 middle-aged mice were not irradiated, but otherwise handled identically and used as sham, unirradiated controls. In this study, all animals were injected with tumor cells, as described below.

Murine Lewis lung carcinoma (LLC) cells, a line originally derived from a spontaneous tumor in a C57BL/6 mouse, were obtained from American Type Culture Collection (Manassas, VA). The LLC cells were cultured under standard conditions in DMEM with high glucose (Gibco Invitrogen Cell Culture, Carlsbad, CA) and 10% FBS (Gibco Invitrogen Cell Culture) and 5% CO2. The measured doubling time for LLC cells was 0.8 days

Tumor Injections
C57BL/6 mice were injected subcutaneously in the mid-dorsal region of the back with 1 x 10^6 LLC cells 8 h after the first irradiation fraction, along with injections of unirradiated control mice.
Mice were prepared for injections by shaving the caudal half of the back and were anesthetized with 4% isoflurane before subcutaneous cell injection of 10^6 LLC cells suspended in 0.2 ml phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Control, sham-irradiated, mice were otherwise treated identically.

Mice were monitored regularly and tumor size was measured with calipers. Once tumors reached approximately 1.5 cm3, mice were euthanized and the tissues were processed. LLC tumor histology was confirmed.

OSD-880.study description: Muscle atrophy is a morbidity and mortality risk factor that happens with disuse, chronic disease, and ageing. Recovery from atrophy involves changes in protein synthesis and different cell types such as muscle fibers, and satellite and immune cells. Here we show that the previously uncharacterized gene and protein Zfp697 is a damage-induced regulator of muscle regeneration. Zfp697/ZNF697 expression is transiently elevated during recovery from muscle atrophy or injury in mice and humans. Sustained Zfp697 expression in mouse muscle leads to a gene expression signature of chemokine secretion, immune cell recruitment, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Myofiber-specific Zfp697 ablation hinders the inflammatory and regenerative response to muscle injury, compromising functional recovery. We uncover Zfp697 as an essential mediator of the interferon gamma response in muscle cells that functions primarily as an ncRNA-binding protein, most notably the pro-regenerative miR-206. This work identifies Zfp697 as an integrator of cell-cell communication necessary for tissue regeneration. Overall design: Comparative gene expression profiling analysis of RNA-seq data for mouse gastrocnemius muscle from model of hindlimb unloading/reloading comparing wild-type and Zfp697 conditional skeletal muscle knockout (mKO) animals. Control mice were kept in conventional cages throughout the entire protocol. Experiment was performed in three replicates per condition.

study protocol description: Generation of a muscle-specific Zfp697 knockout mouse model: Floxed mice for the conditional deletion of the Zfp697 gene were generated on a C57bl6/N background by Biocytogen (USA), using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated homologydirected repair. Briefly, loxP sites were inserted in the intronic region upstream of exon 3 and within the 3´UTR region of exon 3. To minimize the possibility of disrupting Zfp697 expression, both loxP sites were inserted into regions of the gene with low sequence conservation between species. Genomic DNA was extracted from F1 pups and southern blot was used to screen out animals with random insertions. Muscle-specific Zfp697 knockouts (Zfp697-mKO) were generated by crossing Zfp697 floxed mice with animals expressing Cre recombinase under the control of the 1.5-kb Myog promoter and the 1-kb Mef2c enhancer (Myo-Cre; a generous gift from R. Bassel-Duby and E.N. Olson, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, USA). The resulting Zfp697-mKO mice are therefore on a C57bl6/NJ background. Primers for genotyping Zfp697 floxed allele were the following: 5´loxP forward, 5´-TCTGGGACCTGATGAGTCCTACTGG-3´; 5´loxP reverse, 5´-ACGGAGGATAGCCCTTTCTTCCTCA. Hindlimb unloading and reloading: 8-week-old female Zfp697-mKO mice and flox littermates were assigned to three main groups: control, hindlimb unloading or hindlimb reloading. For the hindlimb unloading phase, mice were slightly suspended by tail for the specified number of days, up to 10 days. Briefly, mice were placed inside a restrainer and, using hypoallergenic medical tape, a nylon line was attached in a helical pattern around the base of the tail. The line was connected to a small swivel keychain with metal rings that were attached to a rod running the length of the cage (GR900, Tecniplast). To prevent their hind legs from carrying any weight, the hindlimbs were kept just off the ground with the mouse’s body at an approximately 30-degree angle. Mice were able to move freely on the y-axis, rotate 360-degree using their forelegs, and had access to one side of the cage with food and water ad libitum. Mice were housed in pairs during the unloading phase. The reloading phase consisted of 10 days of hindlimb unloading, after which the animals were returned to normal ambulation in conventional cages for the specified number of days. Control mice were kept in conventional cages throughout the entire protocol with food and water ad libitum. All experiments were approved by the regional animal ethics committee of Northern Stockholm, Sweden.

All tissues were collected, immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80 C until analysis. All experiments were approved by the regional animal ethics committee of Northern Stockholm, Sweden.

Total RNA was extracted from gastrocnemius muscles of mice using TRI reagent (Sigma-Aldrich) as per the manufacturer's instructions. RNA was purified and treated with DNase using NucleoSpin RNA II columns (Machery Nagel) to remove any remaining DNA contaminants. RNA integrity was verified using an Agilent Bioanalyzer, with all samples showing RNA integrity number (RIN) greater than 8.
Stranded mRNA Library Preparation Kit was used with a polyA-enrichment strategy to prepare the sequencing libraries.
RNA-sequencing was performed by the University of Chicago Genomics Facility (Chicago, USA) using the Illumina NovaSeq, generating 100-bp paired-end reads.

Fastq format was checked with fastq_utils v0.25.1. Quality assessment of reads was performed with FastQC v0.12.1 and reports were combined with MultiQC v1.26. rRNA percentages of reads were estimated with the 'hts_SeqScreener' program of htstream v1.3.3 screened against a fasta file of Mus-musculus rRNA sequences retrieved from NCBI on 09-May-2025.

In short, raw fastq files were filtered using Trim Galore! (version 0.6.10) powered by Cutadapt (version 4.2). Trimmed fastq file quality was evaluated with FastQC (version 0.12.1), and MultiQC (version 1.26) was used to generate MultiQC reports. Mus Musculus STAR and RSEM references were built using STAR (version 2.7.11b) and RSEM (version 1.3.3), respectively, Ensembl release 112, genome assembly GRCm39 (Mus_musculus.GRCm39.dna.primary_assembly.fa) and the following gtf annotation file: Mus_musculus.GRCm39.112.gtf. Aligned reads from all samples were quantified using RSEM (version 1.3.3), with strandedness set to forward and RSEM count log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). To create a set of rRNA-removed quantification data, Ensembl IDs mapping to ribosomal RNA (rRNA) were removed from the RSEM gene count data. Both the original set of RSEM quantification data and the rRNA-removed data were subject to differential gene expression analysis as follows. A runsheet was generated with dp_tools (version 1.3.8) and the runsheet and quantification data were imported to R (version 4.4.2) with tximport (version 1.34.0) and normalized with DESeq2 (version 1.46.0) median of ratios method. Normalized gene counts were subject to differential expression analysis. Differential expression analysis was performed in R (version 4.4.2) using DESeq2 (version 1.46.0); all groups were compared pairwise using the Wald test and the likelihood ratio test was used to generate the F statistic p-value. OSD-881.study description: We studied the long-term effects of single whole-body gamma and simulated GCR irradiation (IR) and consumption of a Western Diet (WD) on the heart's right ventricle (RV). Three-month-old C57Bl/6J wild-type male and female mice were assigned to the following groups: 1) Gamma-irradiated with follow-up at 440(males and females) and 660(males)/550(females) days post-IR; 2) simGCRsim-irradiated with follow-up at 440(males and females) and 660(males)/550(females) days post-IR; 3) 270-days WD-fed animals with followup at 530 (males and females) and 750(males)/640(females). Control groups consisted of non-irradiated (non-IR) mice and normal diet-fed mice. Control groups were followed up similarly to the treatment groups.

Animals found spontaneously dead in their cages were grossly examined, and their carcasses were frozen. NSRL GCR and SPE simulations are designed to approximate the chronic mixed field exposures in space by means of sequential acute exposures to a variety of ion/energy combinations. OSD-883.study description: Chemical analysis and other measurements made on lunar-treated plant seedlings grown for 14 to 21 days demonstrate a direct interaction between germfree plants and lunar material. Treated plants dissolved and absorbed significant quantities of Al, Fe, and Ti from the lunar fines. Cabbage and Brussels sprouts were particularly efficient in the dissolution and absorption of Mn. These results suggested that the beneficial effects observed in the Apollo 11 and 12 quarantine studies might be caused by the uptake of ions from the lunar material.

study protocol description:
Seeds to be tested in the Apollo 14 quarantine facilities were obtained from commercial sources and were disinfected with a buffered solution of calcium hypochlorite. The solution was prepared by mixing 174 ml of distilled water, 20 ml of calcium hypochlorite (17 g Ca(OCl)2 dissolved in 100 ml of water), 2.0 ml of 10% triton x-100, and 40 ml of phosphate buffer to adjust the pH to 6.5. This solution was used immediately after preparation to ensure optimum levels of chlorine. For treatment, seeds were placed in a sterile beaker, covered with the disinfectant solution for a 5 -min contact time, and were rinsed 3 times with sterile distilled water. Seed germination tests were
conducted in special slide trays which were filled partially with moistened BR-8, a woodpulp product (produced by the American Can Company) that is stabilized with acrylonitrile, and allowed to air-dry in a sterile room-temp
environment. Ten disinfected seeds of each species were placed in each of 10 chambers; however, for carrots, 15 seeds were used. After treatment with 0.22 g of lunar or terrestrial material, germination was initiated by watering
the slide trays. The planted seeds were kept in total darkness for 2 days then exposed to approximately 8,000 lux with a photoperiod of 16 hr. The temp of the biological containment cabinet was maintained at approximately 23°C. Seeds were
moistened with distilled water for the first 7 days; thereafter, they were watered with a solution of major elements, until the end of the test. Controls consisted of equal numbers of: 1) units treated with sterilized terrestrial material, and 2) untreated units.

An analysis of the lunar and terrestrial materials used in the test Based upon dry wt of the respective samples. Terrestrial material was prepared by the Physical Chemical Section of the Lunar Receiving Laboratory. Samples were ground to pass 105u screen, except lunar sample A which was composed of the particles less than 105u.

The lunar materials were of 2 types: type A, which passed 105-u sieve without grinding, and type B, which passed a 1-mm sieve but
required grinding to pass the 105-u sieve. Type A had a higher glass content, as was reported for fines from Apollo 11 and 12 collections. Both types were classified as lunar-surface “fines”, to designate materials passing a 1-cm sieve without grinding. The terrestrial basalt-ilmenite control was mixed and ground to simulate Apollo 11 fine materials which passed a 105-u sieve. This material was sterilized for 24 hr at 160° C and used in the same manner as the lunar sample. Seeds were germinated on BR-8, a soil substitute, and grown at 23°C for 14 to 21 days. Ten replicates were employed, except for lettuce where six replicates were used for another analysis. One hundred seeds were planted for all but carrot where 150 seeds were used per treatment. The detailed elemental analysis of the treatment growth media is reported in the sample table.

Radish seedlings were collected at 14 days by cutting the stem at the soil line, drying the top portion at 105° C until constant wt was obtained, and then ashing the dry samples. The other seedlings were collected on the
following schedule: cabbage at 17 days, broccoli and lettuce at 18 days, Brussels sprouts at 19 days, and carrots at 21 days. The samples were analyzed by optical
emission spectographic (OES) and atomic absorption spectrophotometric (AAS) techniques.

Calculating Ash Factor: The most satisfactory method for ashing samples to minimize loss of volatile inorganic compounds was the use of a low-temperature asher for 3 to 5 days. The low-temperature asher
operated on the principle of passing oxygen gas at 0.5- to 1-mm pressure through a radio-frequency field, splitting the oxygen into atomic oxygen. The highly active oxygen
reacted with organic material to form gaseous products below 150° C. The gases were pumped away in the vacuum system leaving only oxidized inorganic components of the samples.

The OES technique was used to analyze the following minor and trace elements: B, Fe, Al, Mo, Cu, Co, Zn, Ti, and Ni. The method used was a modification of one reported by Taylor et al. Standards were prepared in a matrix consisting of 100mg Na2C03, 400 mg CaC03, 400 mg K2CO3, and 100 mg MgO. These were made from Johnson-Matthey spectrographic-grade reagents.

Twenty mg of the sample to be tested were mixed with 80 mg of graphite containing 50 ppm palladium. Modifications from Taylor’s method included 8 amperes of arcing time (a complete burn) and the Pd (3460.8 A) line as an internal-standard line.

Any documentation available is contained within supplemental file MMP 21221 - ANALYSIS OF VEGETABLE SEEDLINGS GROWN IN CONTACT WITH APOLLO 14 LUNAR SURFACE FINES.pdf and the publications in the reference list. Due to the historic nature of these experiments some metadata is absent or unclear in the available documentation. At OSDR we welcome contributions from our community. If you review the material associated with this dataset and have a suggestion for an improvement, correction or addition please let us know at arc-dl-osdr-data@mail.nasa.gov.

The AAS technique was used to determine Ca, Mg, Na, K, and Mn. These analyses were performed when there was enough ashed material remaining after the aliquot was taken for the OES technique. Ten mg of ash were dissolved in 2 ml of HCl and diluted to 100 ml with demineralized water.

The methods used for the analysis of each element were those described in the Perkin-Elmer atomic absorption spectrophotometer laboratory manual. Calculations were made using the intensity-ratio method. Concn values were read from previously prepared calibration curves. All final values reported were based on the original weight of the seedlings because they were determined to be as accurate as dry weight.

OSD-888.study description: Despite growing interest in space exploration, the effects of spaceflight on stem cells remain largely unknown. Damages to germline cells are especially crucial, as spaceflight poses risks to gametogenesis, with abnormalities observed in multiple species. While embryonic stem (ES) cells show genomic instability after space exposure and have not yet produced offspring, this study demonstrates successful offspring production from cryopreserved mouse spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs) stored on the International Space Station for 6 months. Spaceflight did not increase apoptosis or DNA damage in SSCs. After thawing, SSCs proliferated comparably to those cryopreserved on Earth, showing no significant phenotypic or functional differences. Offspring were produced via spermatogonial transplantation followed by natural mating. Since SSCs from many species can be cryopreserved like somatic cells and still produce sperm, they offer a promising resource for germline preservation during space exploration.

study protocol description: GS cells used in the present study were previously described (Kanatsu-Shinohara et al., 2003). These cells were derived from C57BL6/Tg14(act-EGFPOsbY01) mice that was bred into DBA/2 background (Okabe et al., 1997). The culture medium for GS cells included GDNF and FGF2, and cells were cultured on MEFs with 1% fetal bovine serum (Kanatsu-Shinohara et al., 2014). For cryopreservation, 1 X 10^6 GS cells were suspended in a cryopreservation solution (1ml; Cellbanker; DIA-IATRON, Tokyo, Japan). After pacing the cryotube (Nunc Biobanking and Cell Culture Cryogenic Tube) in a freezing container (CryoBoxes)(both from Thermo Fisher, MA), cells were frozen at -80°C. These tubes and containers were used in a previous study for ES cells (Yoshida et al., 2024). The samples and PADLES were launched to the ISS by SpaceX CRS-25 (SpX-25) on July 14, 2022, maintaining their frozen status and stored in MELFI at -95°C. After approximately 6 months, the samples were returned to the ground by Spade X CRS-26 (SpX-26) on January 11, 2023, maintaining their frozen status. At the ISS, the frozen vials were kept in MELFI.
The cells were kept at −95 °C during the spaceflight and at −80 °C during transport on Earth.

We thawed the cells and assessed survival using trypan blue staining, with approximately 50%–60% of the cells surviving post-thaw. When Space GS cells were cultured in vitro, their colony morphology was indistinguishable from Ground GS cells, showing grape-like clusters of spermatogonia. The cells were analyzed 14 days after thawing with two rounds of passages. Genomic DNA was harvested using DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit (Qiagen). Genomic DNA was treated with sodium bisulfite, which deaminates unmethylated cytosines to uracils but does not affect 5-methylated cytosines.
Genomic DNA libraries for RRBS were prepared using Zymo-Seq RRBS Library Kit (Zymo Research) following manufacturer's protocols.
Sequencing was done with Illumina NovaSeq X Plus.
Fastq format was checked with fastq_utils v0.25.1. Quality assessment of reads was performed with FastQC v0.11.9 and reports were combined with MultiQC v1.12.

OSD-89.study description: Age plays a crucial role in the interplay between tumor and host; with further perturbations induced by irradiation. Proton irradiation on tumors induces biological modulations including inhibition of angiogenic and immune factors critical to ''hallmark'' processes impacting tumor development, in addition to physical targeting advantages. These advantages have provided promising results for proton therapy in cancer. Additionally, protons have implications for carcinogenesis risk of space travel (due to the high proportion of high energy protons in space radiation). Through a systems biology approach, we investigated how host tissue (i.e. splenic tissue) of tumor-bearing mice is altered with age, with or without whole-body proton exposure. Transcriptome analysis was performed on splenic tissue from adolescent (68 day) versus old (736 day) C57BL/6 male mice injected with Lewis lung carcinoma cells with or without three fractionations of 0.5Gy (1GeV) proton irradiation. Global transcriptome analysis indicated that proton irradiation of adolescent hosts caused significant signaling changes within splenic tissues that support carcinogenesis within the mice, as compared to old subjects. Increases in cell cycling and immunosuppression in irradiated adolescent hosts with CDK2, MCM7, CD74, and RUVBL2 as the key players were involved in the regulatory changes in host environment response (i.e. spleen). These results suggest a significant biological component to proton irradiation, operative through host age, that would indicate a modulation of host's ability to support carcinogenesis in adolescence and the bestowal of resistance to immunosuppression, carcinogenesis, and genetic perturbation by old age.

Murine Lewis lung carcinoma (LLC) cells, originally derived from a spontaneous tumor in a C57BL/6 mouse, were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (Manassas, VA). The LLC cells were cultured under standard conditions in high glucose DMEM (Gibco Invitrogen Cell Culture, Carlsbad, CA) with 10% FBS (Gibco Invitrogen Cell Culture) and 5% CO2.

Tumor Injections:
Injections of C57BL/6 mice were made subcutaneously in the mid-dorsal region of the back with 10^6 LLC cells, 8 h after the first of three dose fractions. Unirradiated mice, serving as controls, were similarly injected with 10^6 LLC cells. Mice were anesthetized by inhalation of 4% isoflurane, for injection of 10^6 LLC cells suspended in 0.2 ml phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Sham mice were treated identically.

Thirty C57BL/6 male mice 68 days old (Jackson Laboratory) and thirty 736 days old (National Institute of Aging) were used in this study, and irradiation protocols of these mice were previously published. Ten adolescent and ten old mice were given whole-body irradiation once a day for three days with 0.5 Gy of proton ions (1-GeV; LET 0.24-keV/µm; plateau, non-Bragg peak, region, 0.5 Gy/min dose rate) at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) (Upton, NY). Mice were restrained and were not anesthetized during irradiation. An additional 20 adolescent and 20 old mice were not irradiated, but otherwise handled identically and used as sham, unirradiated controls. All animals, control and irradiated, were injected with syngeneic LLC cells after the first of three fractions of sham or proton irradiation. The timing of the dosing relative to cancer cell injection was chosen in order to maximize the likelihood of the impact of proton irradiation on tumor development and advancement. This was achieved by combining the situation where the first irradiation fraction acts on the normal cells of the host and later fractions modulate interactions between the host and the cancer cells.

Mice were monitored regularly, and tumor size was measured with calipers by a single individual. Once tumors reached ∼1.5 cm^3 , mice were sacrificed with a 0.6-ml intraperitoneal injection of 2,2,2-tribromoethanol at 20 mg/ml. Tissues to be frozen-sectioned were dissected and slow-frozen in OCT (Tissue Tek, Fisher Scientific, Pittsburgh, PA) in the gas phase of liquid nitrogen, and tissues for RNA isolation were snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen.
OSD-89.study publication title: Proton irradiation impacts age-driven modulations of cancer progression influenced by immune system transcriptome modifications from splenic tissue.

OSD-890.study description: Sequencing optimization experiments using different Oxford Nanopore Technology library preparation methods and input DNA values to determine best method for low-biomass sequencing. This pilot study serves as a technical assessment of wet and dry lab methods for processing and analysis of future NASA cleanroom samples. Microbial standards of known composition were used as input DNA. Data from 4 experiments are provided. The NBD (Native Barcode Kit) experiment utilized the Nanopore Rapid PCR Barcoding Kit 24 V14 and tested nanogram-level input amounts (5ng and 11ng). The three Rapid experiments utilized the Nanopore Rapid PCR Barcoding Kit 24 V14 and tested different input amounts and spike-ins. Rapid1 tested low input amounts (100pg and 500pg), Rapid2 tested ultra-low input amounts (1pg and 10pg), and Rapid3 tested ultra-low input amounts (5pg and 10pg) with and without lambda spike-in. Different data processing pipelines were tested with each set of experimental data as described below. Data from each of the 3 Rapid experiments were processed using 4 different tool combinations for read- and assembly-based processing protocols. The following shows the 4 different combinations tested for the read-based processing approach: Tool combination number, tool used to removed contaminants (blank reads), tool used to remove human reads, tool used for taxonomy assignments, output file suffixes used Test1, Minimap2, Kraken2, Kaiju, “_kraken2-kaiju”, Test2, Minimap2, Kraken2, Kraken2, “_kraken2-kraken2”, Test3, Chopper, Chopper, Kaiju, “_chopper-kaiju”, Test4, Chopper, Chopper, Kraken2, “_chopper-kraken2”. The following shows the 4 different combinations tested for the assembly-based processing approach: Tool combination number, tool used to removed contaminants (blank reads), tool used to remove human reads, tool used for assembly polishing, output file suffixes used: Test1, Minimap2, Kraken2, Medaka, “_kraken2-medaka”, Test2, Minimap2, Kraken2, Minimap2+racon, “_kraken2-racon”, Test3, Chopper, Chopper, Medaka, “_chopper- medaka”, Test4, Chopper, Chopper, Minimap2+racon, “_chopper- racon”. Data from the NBD experiment was processed using 16 different approaches to test different tool combinations, different order of contaminant and human read removal steps, and to test differences in assembling blank reads or not before removing them. Each of the 4 different tool combinations for read- and assembly-based processing protocols described for the Rapid experiments were tested with the NBD data using either unassembled or assembled blank reads, making up 8 different approaches. Those 8 approaches were tested with removing blank reads first followed by human read removal or removing human reads first followed by blank read removal, totaling 16 approaches. The 16 different approaches and respective output file prefixes are detailed in the README.txt file associated with the NBD assay table.
study protocol description: Even- and log-distribution DNA was purchased from Zymo and used for the pilot study as described.
Even distribution: https://www.zymoresearch.com/collections/zymobiomics-microbial-community-standards/products/zymobiomics-microbial-community-dna-standard.
Log distribution: https://www.zymoresearch.com/collections/zymobiomics-microbial-community-standards/products/zymobiomics-microbial-community-dna-standard-ii-log-distribution
All samples were processed immediately and not stored or preserved.

ZymoBIOMICS Microbial Mock Community DNA Standard and DNA Standard II Log Distribution was purchased from Zymo Research and used for MCC Even Distribution and MCC Log Distribution samples, respectively. Quality control metrics and DNA concentration was measured using Qubit fluorometer and Qubit 1x dsDNA HS assay (ThermoFisher Scientific) following the manufacturer's protocol. Samples with lambda DNA contain 100pg of lambda DNA (Oxford Nanopore Technologies, DNA control strand).
Input DNA was 0.005ng or 0.01ng with either 0.1ng lambda spike-in or without lambda spike-in.

DNA libraries were prepared with the Nanopore Rapid PCR Barcoding Kit 24 V14 (Oxford Nanopore Technologies, Oxford, UK) following the manufacturer's protocol with the following modifications: input DNA was 0.005ng or 0.01ng with either 0.1ng lambda spike-in or without lambda spike-in, and 25 PCR cycles were performed. Library quality was assayed for each sample using the High Sensitivity D1000 DNA ScreenTape (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA) following the manufacturer's protocol. All sample libraries were pooled together into one multiplex library. Sample libraries with Qubit values above the detection limit were pooled with eqimolar concentration and if sample libraries were below the Qubit detection limit, the maximum volume (49uL) was used. Multiplex library concentration was measured with Qubit 1x dsDNA HS assay (ThermoFisher Scientific).

The multiplexed DNA libraries (greater than 250 fmol loading concentration) were sequenced with the PromethION 2 Solo system and Minknow Software v25.03.9. 10 hour sequencing time; all other settings default.

Fastq files were generated from the PromethION 2 Solo software using Dorado v7.8.3. Fastq files for each barcode were concatenated into one fastq file per barcode, then quality was assessed with Nanoplot v1.44.1 and reports were summarized with MultiQC v1.27.1.
Quality assessment: Quality assessment of filtered, trimmed, blanks-removed (decontaminated) and human-removed reads was performed with Nanoplot v1.44.1 and reports summarized with MultiQC v1.27.1.

Quality filtering: Raw concatenated reads were filtered by quality (Phred quality greater than or equal to 8) and length (greater than or equal to 200bp) using filtlong v0.2.1. Adapters were then removed from the filtered reads using porechop v0.2.4.
Blanks assembly: Quality controlled blank / negative control sample reads were assembled using Flye v2.9.5.
Blanks reads removal:
Two separate approaches were tested to remove blank reads, one approach used chopper and the other approach used minimap2 followed by samtools, as described below.
Chopper: Blank reads were removed with chopper v0.9.2. Briefly,
assembled blank reads were removed from the quality-filtered/trimmed reads by setting the –contam parameter to the assembled blank contigs.

Minimap2 and samtools: Blank reads were removed using minimap2 v2.2.8 and samtools v1.20. Quality-filtered/trimmed reads were decontaminated by mapping them to the assembled blank contigs using minimap2 v2.2.8 then unmapped/decontaminated reads were filtered out using samtools v1.20 fastq by setting the -f parameter to 4 to retain only unmapped reads.
Human reads removal:

Two separate approaches were tested to remove human reads, one approach started with the chopper-decontaminated reads and used chopper to remove human reads, and the other approach started with the minimap2/samtools-decontaminated reads and used kraken2 to remove human reads, as described below.

Chopper: Human reads were removed with chopper v0.9.2. Briefly, human reads were removed from the chopper-decontaminated reads by setting the –contam parameter to the human genome reference [(GCF_000001405.40) GRCh38.p14]. The human genome reference was downloaded from NCBI's RefSeq database.

Kraken2: Human reads were removed using kraken2 v2.1.6. Human reads were identified and removed from the minimap2/samtools-decontaminated reads using kraken2 v2.1.6 against a human genome reference database that was constructed from NCBI's RefSeq (GCF_000001405.39) GRCh38.p13. The database was constructed by running the kraken build command with the following parameter set --no-masking, --kmer-length 35 and --minimizer-length 31.

Read-based processing: Taxonomy assignment of both sets of blank- and human-removed reads (chopper-chopper and minimap2-kraken2) was performed with Kraken2 v2.1.6 and Kaiju v1.10.1. The resulting assignments were visualized as krona plots using krona v2.8.1.

Assembly-based analysis: Both sets of blank- and human-removed reads (chopper-chopper and minimap2-kraken2) were assembled with Flye v2.9.5 then polished using either medaka v2.0.1 or racon v1.5.0. Genes were called on both sets of polished assemblies with prodigal v2.6.3. Taxonomic classification of genes and contigs was performed with CAT v5.2.3. Functional annotation was done with KOFamScan v1.3.0. Reads were mapped to assemblies with minimap2 v2.2.8, and coverage information was extracted for reads and contigs with samtools v1.20 and bbmap v38.86. Binning of contigs was performed with metabat2 v2.15. Bins were summarized with bit v1.8.53 and estimates of bin quality were generated with checkm v1.1.3. High-quality bins (greater than 90% est. completeness and less than 10% est. redundancy) were taxonomically classified with gtdb-tk v2.4.0 as MAGs (Meta assembled genomes).

Feature table decontamination and visualizations: All graphical displays were conducted using R v4.5.1. Bar plots and heatmaps were generated using R packages ggplot2 v3.5.1 and pheatmap v1.0.13, respectively. Taxonomy and function annotation tables from both read- and assembly-based processing steps were decontaminated with decontam v1.24.0, an R package designed to statistically identify contaminant features in a feature table.

Kraken2: Human reads were removed using kraken2 v2.1.6. Human reads were identified and removed from the minimap2/samtools-decontaminated reads using kraken2 v2.1.6 against a human genome reference database that was constructed from NCBI's RefSeq (GCF_000001405.39) GRCh38.p13. The database was constructed by running the kraken build command with the following parameter set --no-masking, --kmer-length 35 and --minimizer-length 31.

Read-based processing: Taxonomy assignment of both sets of blank- and human-removed reads (chopper-chopper and minimap2-kraken2, with all 4 contaminant removal pipeline permutations as described above) was performed with Kraken2 v2.1.6 and Kaiju v1.10.1. The resulting assignments were visualized as krona plots using krona v2.8.1.

Assembly-based analysis: All sets of blank- and human-removed reads (chopper-chopper and minimap2-kraken2, with all 4 contaminant removal pipeline permutations as described above) were assembled with Flye v2.9.5 then polished using either medaka v2.0.1 or racon v1.5.0. Genes were called on both sets of polished assemblies with prodigal v2.6.3. Taxonomic classification of genes and contigs was performed with CAT v5.2.3. Functional annotation was done with KOFamScan v1.3.0. Reads were mapped to assemblies with minimap2 v2.2.8, and coverage information was extracted for reads and contigs with samtools v1.20 and bbmap v38.86. Binning of contigs was performed with metabat2 v2.15. Bins were summarized with bit v1.8.53 and estimates of bin quality were generated with checkm v1.1.3. High-quality bins (greater than 90% est. completeness and less than 10% est. redundancy) were taxonomically classified with gtdb-tk v2.4.0 as MAGs (Meta assembled genomes).

Feature table decontamination and visualizations: All graphical displays were conducted using R v4.5.1. Bar plots and heatmaps were generated using R packages ggplot2 v3.5.1 and pheatmap v1.0.13, respectively. Taxonomy and function annotation tables from both read- and assembly-based processing steps were decontaminated with decontam v1.24.0, an R package designed to statistically identify contaminant features in a feature table.

OSD-895.study description: The EDEN ISS greenhouse is a space-analog test facility near the German Neumayer III station in Antarctica. The facility is part of the project of the same name and was designed and built starting from March 2015 and eventually deployed in Antarctica in January 2018. The nominal operation of the greenhouse started on February 7th and continued until the 20th of November. The purpose of the facility is to enable multidisciplinary research on topics related to future plant cultivation on human space exploration missions. Research on food quality and safety, plant health monitoring, microbiology, system validation, human factors and horticultural sciences was conducted. Part of the latter is the determination of the biomass production of the different crops. The data on this topic is presented in this dataset. During the first season 26 different crops were grown on the 12.5 m2 cultivation area of the greenhouse. A large number of crops were grown continuously throughout the 9 months of operation, but there were also crops that were only grown a few times for test purposes. The focus of this season was on growing lettuce, leafy greens and fresh vegetables. In total more than 268 kg of edible biomass was produced by the EDEN ISS greenhouse facility in 2018. Most of the harvest was cucumbers (67 kg), lettuces (56 kg), leafy greens (49 kg), and tomatoes (50 kg) complemented with smaller amounts of herbs (12 kg), radish (8 kg), and kohlrabi (19 kg). The environmental set points for the crops were 330 micromole per square meter per second LED light, 21C, a 65% relative humidity, 1000 ppm and the photoperiod was 17 h per day. The overall yearly productivity of the EDEN ISS greenhouse in 2018 was 27.4 kg/m2, which is equal to 0.075 kg/(m2d). This OSD includes data on edible and inedible biomass production of each crop grown in the EDEN ISS greenhouse in Antarctica during the 2018 season.
OSD-895.study funding agency: The EDEN ISS project has received funding from the European Union’s Horizon 2020 Research and Innovation program under grant agreement No 636501.
study protocol description: Crops were cultivated in the Future Exploration Greenhouse (FEG) of the EDEN ISS Mobile Test Facility near Neumayer Station III, Antarctica, during the 2018 experiment phase (first sowing 7 February, final harvest 20 November; 286 days). All crops shared a single compromise climate. Most species were sown in 2 x 2 x 4 cm (L x W x H) rockwool blocks and kept in a nursery tray for 10-20 days (species dependent) before transfer to the plant cultivation trays; parsley, chives and arugula were sown directly in the cultivation trays on recycled cotton fiber mats. Planting density per tray depended on the crop. Cucumber, tomato and pepper were pruned regularly (excess side shoots, old or withered leaves; cucumber trained to 2 stems per plant); basil shoots were shortened when approaching the lamps, and kohlrabi leaves shading neighboring trays were removed. Each cultivation tray had its own independently controlled, liquid-cooled LED lamp (Heliospectra LX601, modified) with a spectrum dominated by blue (~450 nm) and red (~650 nm) light. Photoperiod: 15 h at full intensity with 1 h at 50% intensity before and after (17 h light), followed by 7 h dark. Light intensity measured at 16 cm height: 330 micromole per square meter per second for the four lettuces, red mustard, Swiss chard, mizuna, basil, chives, parsley and arugula (initial setting); 600 micromole per square meter per second
for radish and arugula (higher setting); 300-400 micromole per square meter per second

for tomato, kohlrabi and pepper; greater than 500 micromole per square meter per second at top of canopy for cucumber. Air temperature set points were 21 C during the photoperiod and 19 C during the dark period, relative humidity 65%, and CO2 1000 ppm. Deviations: dark-period temperature dropped to ~16 C during the Antarctic winter; relative humidity reached up to 86% for hours at a time between April and July; CO2 was usually above set point (up to ~2000-4000 ppm) because of operator presence and the absence of a CO2 removal system. Ethylene was scrubbed with an activated carbon filter (target less than 15 ppb; not measured). Each tray was photographed daily from the top and side for remote monitoring.

Nutrient solution was supplied by a hybrid aeroponic/nutrient film technique: high-pressure pumps misted the root zone for 30 s every 6 min, and run-off formed a nutrient film once roots had developed. During germination the on-site operator supplied solution manually. Two solutions were used depending on crop classification, a leafy crop solution and a fruit crop solution, each mixed automatically in bulk tanks from concentrated stock solutions and deionized water. Nutrient parameter values are the expected initial amounts per 100 L of bulk solution. Part way through the mission the fruit crop solution was adjusted to increase calcium and slightly reduce potassium after calcium deficiency was observed on tomato; for the fruit solution, values are given as initial followed by adjusted. pH was controlled with 1.25% nitric acid and 1% potassium hydroxide (tank 1: 6.06 plus or minus 0.18; tank 2: 5.91 plus or minus 0.12). EC set points differed per tank (tank 1: 2.21 plus or minus 0.13 mS/cm; tank 2: 3.49 plus or minus 0.17 mS/cm). Solution temperature followed room temperature (around 19.9 C). Tanks were emptied and refilled with fresh solution approximately every 3 months (tank 1) and every 2 months (tank 2)

Two harvest methods were used. Batch harvest: whole plants were harvested once they reached a set age (lettuces, arugula, radishes, kohlrabi). Spread harvest: only leaves or fruits were removed so the plants continued growing (red mustard, Swiss chard, mizuna, basil, chives, parsley, tomato, cucumber). Sowing, transfer, pruning and harvest dates were recorded for each cultivation tray. At harvest, fresh edible biomass was weighed; inedible biomass was weighed separately for roots and for stems/leaves, and was recovered wet (e.g., roots with rockwool), fresh (e.g., radish leaves) or dry (e.g., withered tomato leaves). Subsamples of plant material were freeze-dried (lyophilized) to determine dry weight ratios; the amount dried was limited by equipment capacity. Most produce was consumed by the overwintering crew, with small amounts set aside for other analyses (e.g., dry weight ratio, nitrate content). Cycles affected by extensive sampling or unsuitable growing procedures were excluded from evaluation; Cycles Evaluated gives the number of valid cycles per crop.

Seeds of most species were sown into 2 x 2 x 4 cm (L x W x H) rockwool blocks placed in a nursery (germination) tray; parsley, chives and arugula were sown directly onto recycled cotton fiber mats in the plant cultivation trays. The on-site operator added small amounts of nutrient solution manually to keep the rockwool blocks moist. Seedlings stayed in the nursery tray for 10-20 days depending on species before being transferred to the cultivation trays. The germination tray was located in the FEG under the same climate set points as the cultivation area. Seed pre-treatment, number of seeds sown, and germination rates were not reported.

For each valid cultivation cycle, edible fresh biomass was normalized to cultivation area (Kilograms per square meter), cultivation time (Kilograms per square meter per day) and cultivation volume (Kilogram per cubic meter). Mean Edible Fresh Weight is the mean edible fresh weight per cultivation area across evaluated cycles, and Edible Fresh Weight Range gives the minimum-maximum (the publication reports mean +/- standard error). Age At Sample Harvest is the average cultivation cycle length. Dry weight (DW) ratio equals mass of lyophilized biomass / original fresh mass (%). Edible Biomass Dry Weight, Inedible Belowground Biomass Dry Weight (roots) and Inedible Aboveground Biomass Dry Weight (stems/leaves; kohlrabi given separately for leaves and skin) are these DW ratios. Aboveground Dry Biomass and Belowground Dry Biomass are the dry inedible biomass of stems/leaves and of roots per cultivation area (grams per square meter; range across measured cycles). Stem/leaf dry biomass measurements for tomato and cucumber were erroneous and are not reported. For fruit crops, the average number of fruits per tray per cycle is given. Over the season the greenhouse produced ~268 kg of fresh edible biomass (27.4 kg/m2 over the 12.5 square meter cultivation area, 0.075 kg/(m2*d)) and ~11.2 kg of dry inedible biomass (excluding miscellaneous crops).

OSD-896.study description: The current report assessed the effects of low-level proton irradiation in inbred adult male Fischer 344 and Lewis rats performing an analog of the human Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT), commonly utilized as an object risk assessment tool to quantify fatigue and sustained attention in laboratory, clinical, and operational settings. These strains were used to determine if genetic differences in dopaminergic function would impact radiation-induced deficits in sustained attention. Exposure to head-only proton irradiation (25 or 100 cGy) disrupted rPVT performance in a strain-specific manner, with 25 cGy-exposed Fischer 344 rats displaying the most severe deficits in sustained attention (i.e., decreased accuracy and increased premature responding); Lewis rats did not display behavioral deficits following radiation. Fischer 344 rats displayed greater tyrosine hydroxylase and dopamine transporter levels in the frontal cortex compared to the Lewis rats, even though radiation exposure increased both of these proteins in the Lewis rats only. Tyrosine hydroxylase was decreased in the parietal cortex of both rat strains following radiation exposure, regardless of proton dose. Strain-specific cytokine changes were also found in the frontal cortex, with the Lewis rats displaying increased levels of putative neurotrophic cytokines (e.g., CNTF). These data support the hypothesis that basal dopaminergic function impacts the severity of radiation-induced deficits in sustained attention. This study derives results from the Western Blot assay using frontal cortex tissue. Results from Western Blot assay using parietal cortex tissue can be found in OSD-897, while results from the Rodent Psychomotor Vigilance Test (rPVT) assay can be found in OSD-939.

study protocol description: Subjects were 17 male Fischer 344 rats (Harlan Laboratories, Indianapolis, Indiana) and 20 Lewis rats, acquired at approximately 10–12 weeks of age. Rats were housed in individual plastic cages and maintained on a 12:12 h light/dark cycle (lights on at 6:00 AM) and at an ambient temperature of 23 degrees Celsius for the duration of the experiment. Rats were run in 30-min rPVT sessions during their light-on cycle at the same time each day in identically constructed operant chambers. Each rPVT chamber contained one nose-poke key, cue lights, a house light, and a food cup for delivery of food pellets. All chambers were contained in sound-attenuating enclosures equipped with an exhaust fan. The weights of the rats were maintained at 85–90 percent of each strain’s free-feeding weight by feeding measured amounts of rat chow each day (30 min after the experimental session, 5 days/week; at similar times on the weekends), in addition to the food that was earned during the behavioral test sessions. Water was freely available in the home cage. Laboratory animal care was according to Public Health Service (PHS) Policy on the Humane Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. This study was carried out in strict accordance with the recommendations in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of the National Institutes of Health. The protocol and all procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the Johns Hopkins University. Johns Hopkins also maintains accreditation of their program by the Association for the Assessment and Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care (AAALAC).

Rats were exported to Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) for radiation exposure 4–5 days prior to the scheduled exposure day. All animals were exposed on the same day, and then returned to Johns Hopkins for follow-up testing 4–5 days following exposure. While at BNL, rats were maintained under housing conditions similar to those at JHU, including the same light/dark cycle and were individually housed in plastic cages with a water bottle, wire top, and insulator top, that were filled with bedding and contained enrichment toys (i.e., Nyla bones). Rats also received ad lib access to water and food while at BNL. The control group was sham-irradiated, i.e., shipped to BNL, sedated and restrained for radiation exposure, but not actually exposed. The remaining rats were irradiated with 150 MeV/n protons generated at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) facility at BNL. Protons of this energy have a mean range in water of approximately 15.5 cm with an average LET of 0.4 keV/um. Target exposure levels were 25 and 100 cGy; actual delivered doses varied by no more than +/- 0.1 cGy relative to each target dose. Dose rates ranged from 30–71 cGy/min to achieve an even dose distribution across the collimated exposure field. Irradiation involved head-only exposures to minimize systemic responses to exposures that can confound morphological, neurochemical, and behavioral testing. For radiation exposures, rats received an intraperitoneal injection (2 ml/kg administered volume) of ketamine (90 mg/kg) and xylazine (5 mg/kg) and were subsequently placed in a ventilated polystyrene holder (2 rats/holder). Each body was shielded by a specially built trilaminar collimator exposure system consisting of Plexiglas, aluminum, and polyurethane; the body dose was less than 2 percent of the delivered dose.

To determine the levels of various proteins in the brain following radiation exposure and behavioral testing, all rats were sacrificed at approximately 9-months (35–36 weeks) post-exposure. Whole rat brains were excised after decapitation, frontal and parietal cortices dissected, flash frozen, and immediately stored at -80 degrees Celsius until processed.

Whole rat brains were excised after decapitation, frontal and parietal cortices dissected, flash frozen, and immediately stored at -80 C until processed. Tissue sections were weighed and placed in a 1.5 ml centrifuge tube. Tissue was homogenized on ice using 3 ml of Radio Immuno Precipitation Assay (RIPA) buffer containing complete protease inhibitor and phophastase inhibitors per gram of tissue. Samples were then centrifuged at 12,000 x g for 10 min at 4°C, the pellet was discarded and the lysate transferred to a new microtube. Lysates were again centrifuged at 12,000 x g for 10 min at 4C. The supernatant from the second centrifugation contains total protein lysate that was used for Western Blotting. Protein concentrations were calculated from each sample using Biorad Protein Assay Dye. 20 ug of total protein from each rat were loaded onto 4–12% Bis-Tris gels and electrophoresed for 90 minutes at 110 volts in MOPS running buffer.
Proteins were then electrophoretically transferred for 80 min at 30V onto PVDF membrane and subsequently incubated in Ponceau reagent for 10 minutes to ensure complete transfer of all proteins.
After transfer, the membrane was blocked in 5% Non-fat dry milk in 1x Tris buffered saline containing 0.1% Tween 20 (TBST).
Membranes were incubated with primary antibodies in TBST buffer for one hour at room temperature.

The primary antibodies used were: Akt 1:1000; pAktser473 1:1000; tyrosine hydroxylase (TOH) 1:500; pCREB 1:1000; dopamine transporter (DAT) 1:700; beta-actin, 1:2000. Membranes were washed (3 x 10 minutes) in TBST. Incubation with secondary antibody was performed at a dilution of 1:2500.
Incubation with secondary antibody was performed at a dilution of 1:2500.

After additional washing steps, West Dura chemilluminescence substrate was added to the membranes and they were allowed to incubate for 5 minutes. Membranes were visualized using a digital ChemiDoc-It imaging system. Densitometry was performed on all western blots and signal normalized to beta-actin, which serves as a housekeeping gene. For each protein, densitometry was calculated, and ratios of each protein/beta actin were calculated for individual rats in each proton dose level group. These protein/actin ratios were compared between sham-irradiated controls of each strain with independent-samples t-tests to determine if strain differences were apparent. To enable between strain comparisons in the event of strain difference between sham controls, rats’ protein/actin ratios were normalized to their strain-specific sham-irradiated control group, which were both set to 1.

To enable maximal data reuse (for machine-readable approaches), the submitted version of this dataset was subsequently transformed and edited to be aligned with a reusable template, which was created through feedback provided by subject matter experts in the ALSDA Analysis Working Group. This transformed reusable version is structured so all results are standardized into specific rows (source/subject) and columns (measures). This enables all assay results to be identically structured for efficient data mining. Please refer to the study-level data dictionary file for a complete list of column header names and descriptions.

OSD-898.study description: Many factors contribute to the health risks encountered by astronauts on missions outside Earth’s atmosphere. Spaceflight-induced potential adverse neurovascular damage and late neurodegeneration are a chief concern. The goal of the present study was to characterize the effects of spaceflight on oxidative damage in the mouse brain and its impact on blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity. Ten-week-old male C57BL/6 mice were launched to the International Space Station (ISS) for 35 days as part of Space-X 12 mission. Ground control (GC) mice were maintained on Earth in flight hardware cages. Within 38 ± 4 hours after returning from the ISS, mice were euthanized and brain tissues were collected for analysis. Quantitative assessment of brain tissue demonstrated that spaceflight caused an up to 2.2-fold increase in apoptosis in the hippocampus compared to the control group. Immunohistochemical analysis of the mouse brain revealed an increased expression of aquaporin4 (AQP4) in the flight hippocampus compared to the controls. There was also a significant increase in the expression of platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule-1 (PECAM-1) and a decrease in the expression of the BBB-related tight junction protein, Zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1). These results indicate a disturbance of BBB integrity. Quantitative proteomic analysis showed significant alterations in pathways responsible for neurovascular integrity, mitochondrial function, neuronal structure, protein/organelle transport, and metabolism in the brain after spaceflight. Changes in pathways associated with adhesion and molecular remodeling were also documented. These data indicate that long-term spaceflight may have pathological and functional consequences associated with neurovascular damage and late neurodegeneration. This study derives results from Microscopy assays.

study protocol description:
SpaceX-12 was launched in 2017 at the Kennedy Space Center (KSC) on a 35-day mission. Ten-week-old male C57BL/6 mice
(n equals 20) (Jackson laboratories, Inc Bar Harbor, ME) at the time of launch, were flown for NASA’s ninth Rodent Research experiment (RR-9) and lived in NASA’s Rodent Habitats (RH) aboard the International Space Station (ISS). All flight (FLT) mice were maintained at an ambient temperature of 26-28 degrees Celsius with a 12-hour light/dark cycle during the flight. Habitat ground control (GC) mice (n equals 20) were kept under similar housing conditions, including temperature, humidity, and carbon dioxide (CO2) levels using 48-hour delayed telemetry data from the FLT group. Water and food bar diet specifically designed by NASA were provided ad libitum to FLT and GC groups. All mice received the same access to food and water. There were no significant changes in body weight before and after the mission for FLT and GC groups. NASA-Ames Research Center and KSC Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees approved this flight study. The study has been done in strict accordance with the recommendations in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of the National Institute of Health (NIH).

Within 38 plus or minus 4 hours of splashdown, the FLT mice were rapidly euthanized in 100% CO2. The GC mice were euthanized with the same method after 38 days of GC housing. Shortly after euthanasia, brains were removed and bisected along the midline. The left hemi-brains were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde in phosphate buffered saline (PBS)
for 24 hours and then, rinsed with PBS, infiltrated overnight with 30% sucrose in PBS at 4 degree Celsius, and then, embedded in optimal cutting temperature (OCT) compound and frozen at -80 degree Celsius for IHC and apoptosis assays. Brains were then sectioned coronally at a thickness of 20 μm unless otherwise indicated. Five systematically selected sections from each brain sample were used for each biomarker staining.

The left hemi-brains were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde in phosphate buffered saline (PBS) for 24 hours and then, rinsed with PBS, infiltrated overnight with 30% sucrose in PBS at 4 degrees Celsius and then, embedded in optimal cutting temperature (OCT) compound and frozen at −80 degrees Celsius for IHC and apoptosis assays. Brains were then sectioned coronally at a thickness of 20 um unless otherwise indicated. Five systematically selected sections from each brain sample were used for each biomarker staining.

Sections were incubated with anti-4-HNE antibody (Alpha Diagnostic International Inc, San Antonio, TX, USA) at 48 C for 2 hours followed by a fluorescence-conjugated donkey anti-rabbit IgG (catalog no. A21206, Invitrogen Corp. Waltham, MA, USA) for 2 hours at room temperature and counterstained with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) (Invitrogen, Eugene, Oregon, USA).

The mean of the fluorescence intensity profile measurements across five sections per cortex or hippocampus was used as a single experimental value. Data were then extracted and averaged within the hippocampus or cortex across the group.

OSD-899.study description: The objective of the Rodent Research-10 mission (RR-10) was to investigate how spaceflight affects the cellular and molecular mechanisms of normal bone tissue regeneration in space. To this end, ten (10) 14-15 weeks-old female B6129SF2/J Wild Type (WT), and ten (10) 14-15 weeks-old female B6;129S2-Cdkn1atm1Tyj/J (p21-null) mice received a pre-flight subcutaneous injection of the bone marker (Alizarin Red), and were then delivered to the ISS aboard SpaceX-21. At 7 days before euthanasia, all 20 mice received an intraperitoneal (IP) injection with a bone formation marker (Calcein). At 48 +/- 2 hours before euthanasia, all 20 mice received an IP injection with a second dose of Calcein as well as a cell proliferation marker (BrdU). Then, following 28-29 days in microgravity, the Flight mice were euthanized. Following removal of hindlimbs, carcasses were wrapped in aluminum foil, preserved in the CryoChiller, and stored at -80 C or colder until return to Earth. In addition to the Flight group, three ground control groups were also part of the study: Basal (representing the pre-launch state), Vivarium (standard vivarium housing for the same duration of time as flight), and Ground (flight habitat in the International Space Station Environment Simulator, ISSES). Twenty mice (10 of each strain) were included in each of these control groups (except Vivarium which included 12 of each strain). These were treated, euthanized and processed on the same schedule and in the same manner as the flight samples. This study includes bulk RNA sequencing ribodepleted gene expression data from the cecum of 20 Basal animals (10 WT and 10 p21-null), 10 Flight animals (5 WT and 5 p21-null), 10 Ground animals (5 WT and 5 p21-null), and 24 Vivarium animals (12 WT and 12 p21-null).
OSD-899.study funding agency: The sequencing analysis was funded by the NASA Space Biology program within the NASA Science Mission Directorate's (SMD) Biological and Physical Sciences (BPS) Division.

This mission examined how aging influences the regenerative potential of the femoral bone marrow stem cell populations. Specifically, the study examined the role of a gene – Cdkn1a – that produces the CDKN1A protein – that inhibits cell cycle progression in cells. RR-10 (20 female mice, 13-17 weeks old, B6129SF2/J Wild Type (WT) and B6;129S2-Cdkn1atm1Tyj/J (p21-null) to assess the CDKN1a/p21 pathway in regenerative bone formation. The mice will be maintained on the ISS for ~30 days. In addition to the Flight group, three ground control groups were also part of the study: Basal (representing the pre-launch state), Vivarium (standard vivarium housing for the same duration of time as flight), and Ground (flight habitat in the International Space Station Environment Simulator, ISSES). At the end of RR-10 experiment, all frozen carcasses and preserved hindlimbs were returned to the PI. In May 2021, the Biospecimen Sharing Program (BSP) team performed complex, integrated dissections at NASA Ames Research Center with the Principal Investigator team. Cecem tissues were kept at -80C freezer until processing. Baseline dissections were performed 7 days after launch following the same procedures used for the Flight animals.

RNA was extracted using the AllPrep DNA/RNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA) following GeneLab SOP 3.1-Qiagen AllPrep DNA/RNA Mini with Qiagen RNase-Free DNase set. Homogenization buffer for RNA purification was made by adding 1:100 beta-mercaptoethanol to Buffer RLT (Qiagen, Valencia, CA) and kept on ice until use. Approximately 20 mg of tissue was isolated using a scalpel, weighed, and immediately placed in 700 uL of the Buffer RLT solution. Homogenization was performed using tissue homogenizing bead mix red, (Next Advance, Raymertown, NY) on Bullet Blender Gold 24 (Next Advance, Raymertown, NY) for 3 minutes at 4 C per SOP 2.1-Tissue homogenization Using Bullet Blender Gold Bead Beater. Homogenates were centrifuged for 5 minutes at RT and 14,000 g to remove cell debris. The supernatant from each sample was then used to isolate and purify DNA and RNA following the manufacturer protocol. RNA was eluted in 35 uL RNAse free H2O, and DNA was eluted in 50 uL RNAse free H2O. Concentration for all RNA samples were measured using Qubit 3.0 Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA) with Qubit RNA BR kit following SOP 4.1-RNA/DNA/miRNA/cDNA Quantification using Qubit Fluorimeter. RNA quality was assessed using the Agilent 4200 TapeStation with the Agilent RNA ScreenTape (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA). DNA quality and size were assessed using the Agilent 4200 TapeStation with Agilent gDNA ScreenTape Kit (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA). GeneLab Sample Processing SOP can be found at the GitHub page, https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab-sampleProcessing/tree/master/SOP_docs

ERCC ExFold RNA Spike-In Mixes (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, Cat 4456739, v92), Mix 1 or Mix 2, were added on the day of library prep at the concentrations suggested by the manufacturer protocol. SOP 5.2 Use of ERCC Spike-In Mixes and UMRR/UHRR Controls for Total RNA Sequencing. GeneLab Sample Processing SOP can be found at the GitHub page, https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab-sampleProcessing/tree/master/SOP_docs.

RNA ribo depletion and library preparation was done with Illumina TruSeq Stranded Total RNA Library Prep Gold (Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA) following GeneLab SOP 5.1 Ilumina TruSeq Stranded Total RNA Lirary Prep using epMotion. Input RNA were approximately 500 ng with RIN greater than 4. Index adapters used were at 1.5 uM ( ILMN TruSeq RNA UD Indexes V2, lot

20958275). 15 cycles PCR were performed. Library fragment size was assessed using Agilent 4200 TapeStation with D1000 DNA ScreenTape (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA) following GeneLab SOP 6.3 Quality analysis of sequencing libraries using 4200 TapeStation System with D1000 reagent kit. Pooled library concentration was measured by Qubit 4 Fluorometer (ThermoFisher Scentific, Waltham, MA) following SOP 4.1-RNA/DNA/miRNA/cDNA Quantification using Qubit Fluorimeter. Library quality assessment was performed on iSeq100 (Illumina, San Diego, CA). GeneLab Sample Processing SOP can be found at the GitHub page, https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab-sampleProcessing/tree/master/SOP_docs.

RNA sequencing was performed by GeneLab Sample Processing Lab on Illumina NovaSeq 6000. Sequencing was set up as following: Read 1: 151 bp, Index1: 10 bp, Index2: 10 bp, Read 2: 151 bp. PhiX v3 was included as control and to increase library diversity. Protocol followed is SOP 7.1-Setting up NovaSeq 6000 and iSeq 100 Sequencers. GeneLab Sample Processing SOP can be found at the GitHub page, https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab-sampleProcessing/tree/master/SOP_docs.

Quality assessment of reads was performed with FastQC v0.12.1 and reports were combined with MultiQC v1.26. rRNA percentages of reads were estimated with the 'hts_SeqScreener' program of htstream v1.3.2 screened against a fasta file of M. musculus rRNA sequences retrieved from NCBI on 09-05-2025.

Data were processed as described in GL-DPPD-7101-G (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/master/RNAseq/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7101_Versions/GL-DPPD-7101-G.md), using NF_RCP version 2.1.0 (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_RNASeq_Workflow/tree/NF_RCP_2.1.0). In short, raw fastq files were filtered using Trim Galore! (version 0.6.10) powered by Cutadapt (version 4.2). Trimmed fastq file quality was evaluated with FastQC (version 0.12.1), and MultiQC (version 1.26) was used to generate MultiQC reports. Mus Musculus STAR and RSEM references were built using STAR (version 2.7.11b) and RSEM (version 1.3.3), respectively, Ensembl release 112, genome assembly GRCm39 (Mus_musculus.GRCm39.dna.primary_assembly.fa) concatenated with ERCC92.fa from ThermoFisher (https://assets.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/LSG/manuals/ERCC92.zip), and the following gtf annotation file: Mus_musculus.GRCm39.112.gtf concatenated with the ERCC92.gtf file from ThermoFisher (https://assets.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/LSG/manuals/ERCC92.zip). Trimmed reads were aligned to the Mus Musculus + ERCC STAR reference with STAR (version 2.7.11b) and alignment log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). Aligned reads were assessed for strandedness using RSeQC infer_experiment.py (version 5.0.4), gene body coverage using RSeQC geneBody_coverage.py (version 5.0.4), inner distance was assessed using RSeQC inner_distance.py (version 5.0.4), and distribution of RNA features using RSeQC read_distribution.py (version 5.0.4). Aligned reads from all samples were quantified using RSEM (version 1.3.3), with strandedness set to reverse and RSEM count log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). A runsheet was generated with dp_tools (version 1.3.8) and the runsheet and quantification data were imported to R (version 4.4.2) with tximport (version 1.34.0) to generate the RSEM raw counts data. A set of rRNA-removed raw counts data was also created by removing Ensembl IDs that map to ribosomal RNA (rRNA) from the RSEM gene count data. Assessment of ERCC spiked genes was performed as detailed in the ERCC_analysis_GLbulkRNAseq.html report.

Two-condition experiment, mock irradiated vs. cells exposed to activated medium. 3 biological replicates were independently grown and harvested during three different runs at the NSRL. One replicate per array.

study protocol description: RNA was extracted using a modified guanidine thiocyanate method (Chomczynski and Sacchi, 1987, PMID: 2440339) followed by purification with RNeasy columns (Qiagen, Valencia, CA).
RNA samples were quantified using a Nanodrop spectrophotometer and monitored for quality using an Agilent Bioanalyzer prior to labeling for microarray analysis.

Fluorescently labeled cDNA was prepared from mock-irradiated control and activated medium control whole-cell RNA by a single round of reverse transcription (BRL Superscript II) in the presence of aminoallyl dUTP (Sigma-Aldrich), followed by coupling to monofunctional NHS-ester Cy3 or Cy5 dye (Amersham) (Amundson and Fornace, 2004. PMID:14970650)

Hybridization was carried out with active mixing using the MAUI Hybridization System (BioMicro Systems, Salt Lake City, UT) for 16 hours in Deposition Hybridization Buffer (Agilent) at 65oC in the presence of the blockers human CoT1, yeast tRNA and poly dA.
Hybridized slides were washed at room temperature once in 0.5X SSC, 0.01% SDS for 5 minutes and again in 0.06X SSC for 5 minutes.

Slides were scanned on an Agilent Microarray Scanner, 100% PMT voltage, 10 uM resolution scans. Images were processed using ArraySuite 2.1 extensions in the IPLab program (Scanalytics Inc., Fairfax, VA) as described in Chen et al., 2002 (PMID: 12217912).

TK6 cells were maintained in exponential growth at densities of 1-10 x 10^5 cells/ml in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated (56C for 45 minutes) fetal calf serum and 100 U/ml penicillin and 100 U/ml streptomycin in a humidified, 5% CO2 atmosphere in a 37C incubator.
HZE particle irradiation was performed at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) at Brookhaven National Laboratory.

Exponentially growing cells were concentrated by centrifugation and exposed to graded doses of 1 GeV/amu 56Fe ions (148 keV/um) in a volume of 10 ml per culture point to limit the amount of medium activated during the irradiation.
Dosimetry was performed by the NSRL Physics Group.

Tubes containing the cells were placed perpendicular to the beam in the center of the field, where the variation in fluence was less than 5%. Control cultures were prepared in the same way and mock irradiated.
An activated-medium control was prepared by irradiating 10 ml of medium without cells to the highest dose used (2.5 Gy).
Immediately after irradiation, medium was added to bring the cells to normal culture densities (4-5 x 10^5cells/ml).
The cells for the activated control were resuspended in the activated medium prior to addition of the remaining medium.

OSD-90.project title: The Effect of Microgravity on Mycobacteria
OSD-90.study description: The aim of this work is to determine whether mycobacteria have enhanced virulence during space travel and what mechanisms they use to adapt to microgravity. M. marinum and LHM4 were grown in high aspect ratio vessels (HARV) in a rotary cell culture system (RCCS) under normal gravity (NG) or low shear simulated microgravity (MG). To determine the effect of MG on the stress responses activated by the growth conditions, we used RNAseq to examine what genes were expressed. For RNAseq, the bacteria are harvested, RNA isolated and converted DNA (cDNA), and the cDNA sequenced. Using bioinformatics, the amount of expression of the different M. marinum genes were compared between the NG and MG samples. To make sure that we were examining only gene expression changes due to MG, only bacteria in early exponential growth were used in the RNAseq studies. Triplicate NG and MG cultures were used to generate samples of bacteria grown for ~40 hrs. We also grew triplicate cultures for 4 days and then diluted them again and grew them for another ~40 hrs so we could examine gene expression from bacteria exposed for a longer time. In summary, this study determined that waterborne mycobacteria alter their growth, expression of stress responses, and their sensitivity to oxidizing conditions when subjected to growth under MG.
OSD-90.study funding agency: This study was funded by the NASA Space Biology Program Office, Space Life and Physical Sciences Research and Applications Division (2012 Space Biology NNH12ZTT001N).
study protocol description: M. marinum strain 1218R, a strain isolated from infected fish, was used for this study. Bacteria were grown in the dark at 30 C in tubes in a rotating incubator (120 r.p.m.) or in HARVs attached to a rotating cell culture system (RCCS, Synthecon, Houston, TX, USA) in Middlebrook 7H9 broth (Difco, Detroit, MI, USA) supplemented with ADS (5% BSA Fraction V, 2% Dextrose, 0.81% NaCl) to 10%, 0.5% glycerol, 100 ug cycloheximide/ml, and 0.2% Tween 80. Cultures were also grown on solid Middlebrook 7H10 agar (Difco) supplemented with 10% ADS, 0.5% glycerol, and 100ug cycloheximide/ml. To initiate cultures, solid medium was inoculated from a frozen stock and incubated for ~7 days to obtain colonies. Colonies were used to inoculate tube cultures (~3 ml). The tube cultures were grown for 5–7 days to an OD600 ~1. This tube culture was then diluted to OD600 0.0005 or 0.002 before growth in 10 or 50 ml HARVs, respectively. The lower OD600 of the culture at the start of growth in the 10 ml HARVs prevented the cultures from being at saturation density for the majority of the 4-day exposure time. For the short exposure time, the cultures were grown in 50 ml HARVs. For the long exposure, the cultures were grown in 10 ml HARVs for 4 days and then re-diluted to OD600 0.002 in 50 ml HARVs for another ~35 h. For NG, HARVs were rotated (25 r.p.m.) on an axis parallel to the direction of gravitational force, while they were rotated (25 r.p.m.) on an axis perpendicular to the direction of the gravitational force for LSMMG.

Bacteria were exposed to either normal gravity (NG) or low shear modeled microgravity (LSMMG) for either ~40 hrs (short exposure) or for 4 days prior to re-dilution and exposure for a further ~36 hrs (long exposure). It was necessary to re-dilute the 4 day culture to make sure that the bacteria were all in the same phase of growth when RNA was prepared from the culture.

The RNA was DNase-treated and purified through an RNeasy MinElute Cleanup kit prior to determination of the concentration using the Quibit 2.0 RNA BR (Broad-Range) assay and RNA integrity score (RIN) using the Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer, RNA 6000 Nano assay.

Ribosomal RNA was removed from approximately 4.6 micrograms of total RNA using the Ribo-Zero Magnetic Kit for Bacteria (Epicentre, an Illumina company, Madison, WI) following the manufacturer's instructions. The rRNA-depleted RNA was purified using the RNeasy MinElute Cleanup Kit (QIAGEN, Germantown, MD). The quality of the rRNA-depleted RNA was estimated using an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer RNA Pico chip. The ScriptSeq v2 kit (Epicentre) was used to prepare stranded and indexed RNA-Seq libraries.

Briefly, rRNA-depleted RNA was chemically fragmented, and cDNA was synthesized from a tagged random hexamer. The cDNA was terminal tagged using a 3′-end blocked and tagged oligo followed by purification on a MinElute column. The di-tagged cDNA was then used as template for PCR (15 cycles) using the FailSafe PCR Enzyme (Epicentre), a forward primer and an indexed/barcoded reverse primer. The amplified libraries were purified using Agencourt AMPure XP beads (Beckman Coulter, Indianapolis, IN) resulting in an average library size of approximately 350 base pairs when assessed on an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer High Sensitivity DNA chip. Libraries were quantitated using a Qubit Double Stranded DNA High Sensitivity assay.
Libraries were normalized to 4 nM, pooled, denatured, and diluted to approximately 6 pM.
A 1% library of 20 pM PhiX was spiked in as an internal control.
The library pool was sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq (Illumina, San Diego, CA) using v3 chemistry and a paired-end read length of 2 x 76 base pairs.
Base calling and quality scoring were performed with Illumina Real Time Analysis software.

Fastq format was checked with fastq_utils v0.25.1. Quality assessment of reads was performed with FastQC v0.11.9 and reports were combined with MultiQC v1.12. rRNA percentages of reads were estimated with the 'hts_SeqScreener' program of htstream v1.3.3 screened against a fasta file of Mycobacterium rRNA sequences retrieved from NCBI on 09-May-2025.

This study includes bulk RNA sequencing ribodepleted gene expression data from the lungs of 12 Basal animals (6 WT and 6 p21-null), 10 Flight animals (5 WT and 5 p21-null), 10 Ground animals (5 WT and 5 p21-null), and 10 Vivarium animals (5 WT and 5 p21-null).
