study protocol description: Rodent Research Reference Mission 1 (RRR-1) / Rodent Research-8 (RR-8) consisted of 40 BALB/cAnNTac females (8 used for this study) termed Flight which were sent on 12/5/2018 to the International Space Station (ISS), and a control group of 40 mice remained on Earth, termed Habitat Ground Control (HC). Furthermore, two age groups were used, younger (∼3 months) and older (∼8 months). All mouse work was completed with approval of the NASA Flight Animal Care and Use Committee (Protocol

FLT-18-116). Mice were received following landing at Scripps Research Institute (09-0004, for animal receipt upon landing) and transported to Stanford University IACUC (WYS1591). Flight mice were housed at double density on launch and again during the return to earth. HC mice were housed to match, as closely as possible, conditions experienced by Flight mice. This included double density housing in identical Mouse Habitat Units and Transporters as used by NASA during launch for Flight mice, and matched temperature, humidity, and carbon dioxide levels (elevated on the ISS compared to Earth) based on actual flight environmental monitoring. All mice were adapted to NASA Nutrient Food Bars, four weeks prior to launch, and bars were exchanged weekly. Mice had ad libitum access to both food and water. Mice had ad libitum access to both food and water. During the mission we encountered the following issues, altering the planned experimental design, or that must be considered upon interpretation of results. (1) Within 24h of the planned launch, mold was found on the food bars, affecting both Flight and HGC mice to an unknown degree. It is possible that the mice were able to eat around the mold. The late replacement of the food bars, now secured with double-sided tape instead of epoxy, caused the bars to free-float during launch and return. The bars of the HGC mice fell to the bottom of the cage. Although the Flight mice appeared healthy upon arrival to the ISS, this might have induced additional stress. Due to concerns about mold, as more was discovered aboard the ISS, the ISS Term mice were sacrificed after approximately 3 weeks of microgravity rather than the planned 8 weeks, and ground controls were sacrificed to match this new timeline.(2) Due to poor weather, the return of the Flight LAR mice was delayed and the mice spent 7 instead of the normal 2-3 days in double density housing. This housing is more confined (10 mice per cage side instead of the 5 in the normal habitat), video monitoring was not possible and food bars likely became unsecured and were free-floating. Conditions of the HGC mice were matched to these conditions, likely causing additional stress for both groups. Due to the weather, the Flight group likely experienced rough seas upon splashdown and shipping back to shore, which was not controlled for in the HGC group.

HC mice were shipped to Scripps Institute just prior to the return of the Flight mice so that all mice could be dissected together in matching conditions (+/- 1 day). The mice from the Flight group were returned alive to Earth on 1/14/2019 after 39.5 days on the ISS and collected 2-4 days after splashdown following functional assays at Scripps Research Institute. In this study, fresh organ samples were obtained and immediately processed from 8 live mice that arrived at Stanford University from Scripps Research Institute on 1/16/2019. Two mice each from the following groups were included: Flight 3mo, Flight 8mo, HC 3mo, HC 8mo. All four Flight mice were dissected on 1/16/2019 to minimize time spent outside of microgravity, and all four HC mice dissected on 1/17/2019. LAR mice were anesthetized with gas anesthesia and euthanized by means of cardiac
puncture blood draw (exsanguination) and double thoracotomy.

All the tissues were processed as previously described (https://doi.org:10.1038/s41586-020-2496-1). Isolated bones from forelimbs, hindlimbs, hips, and vertebrae were crushed in FACS buffer (2% sterile FBS in PBS) on ice, filtered through a 100 um strainer (Falcon 352360), pelleted (300 x g, 4C, 5 minutes), and resuspended in FACS buffer with 100 U/ml DNase I (Worthington LS006344) and 20 ug/ml Rat-IgG (Abcam ab37361) for 10 minutes on ice. Cells were incubated with anti-CD117 MicroBeads (Miltenyi Biotec 130-091-224) on ice for 20 minutes, pelleted, resuspended in FACS buffer, and filtered through a 40 um strainer (Falcon 352340) into an LS column (Miltenyi Biotec 130-042-401). Following magnetic purification, c-Kit+ cells were eluted, and the flow through was depleted of RBCs with Histopaque-1119 (Sigma-Aldrich RNBF0417). The c-Kit+ cells and RBC-depleted flow through were resuspended in FACS buffer with Rat-IgG (20 ug/mL) and incubated on ice for 10 minutes. The flow-through was stained for B-cells, T-cells, and granulocytes. All antibodies were used at 1:50. c-Kit+ cells were stained with CD3-FITC (BioLegend 133301, clone 17A2), Ly-6G/Ly-6C/GR1-FITC (BioLegend 133301, clone RB6-8C5), CD11B/MAC1-FITC (BioLegend 133301, clone M1/70), CD45R/B220-FITC (BioLegend 133301, clone RA3-6B2), TER119-FITC (BioLegend 133301), CKIT-APC (BioLegend 105812, clone 2B8), SCA-1-PECy7 (BioLegend 122514, clone E13-161.7). B-cells were stained with TER119-PECy5 (BioLegend 116210), B220-FITC (BioLegend 103206, clone RA3-6B2), IgM-PECy7 (BioLegend 406514, clone RMM-1). T-cells were stained with TER119-PECy5 (BioLegend 116210), CD90/Thy1.1-AF488 (BioLegend 202506, clone OX-7), CD90/Thy1.2-FITC (BioLegend 140304, clone 53-2.1), CD2-PECy7 (BioLegend 100114, clone RM2-5). Granulocytes were stained with TER119-PECy5 (BioLegend 116210), CD11B/MAC1-FITC (BioLegend 101206, clone M1/70), Ly-6G/Ly-6C/GR1-PECy7 (BioLegend 108416, clone RB6-8C5). Cells were incubated in antibody for 20 minutes, washed with FACS buffer, and pelleted (300 x g, 4C, 5 minutes). After resuspension in FACS buffer, cells were filtered into 35 um FACS tubes (Falcon 352235) and stained with 1:1000 SYTOX Blue (ThermoFisher S34857) immediately prior to sorting.

Cells were loaded in each channel with a target output of up to 5,000 cells per sample, though fewer cells were captured for small sample types. scRNA-seq libraries were constructed following the 10x Genomics protocol using the GemCode Single-Cell 3’ Gel Bead and Library v3 Kit. All reactions were performed in a Biorad C1000 Touch Thermal Cycler with a 96-Deep Well Reaction Module. Twelve cycles were used for cDNA amplification and sample index PCR. Amplified cDNA and final libraries were evaluated on a Fragment Analyzer using a High Sensitivity NGS Analysis Kit (Advanced Analytical). Library preparation was performed one organ type at a time, in sets of eight samples. Within each organ set, cDNA was normalized, and 13–20 PCR cycles were run depending on cDNA amount. The average fragment length of 10x cDNA libraries was quantified on a Fragment Analyzer (AATI) and by qPCR using the Kapa Library Quantification Kit for Illumina. Each library was diluted to 4 nM, and equal volumes were pooled for each sequencing run.

Sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform using 100-cycle run kits, with 28 bases for Read 1, 8 bases for Index 1, and 91 bases for Read 2 (Illumina 20012862). A PhiX control library was spiked in at 0.2–1%.

Fastq format was checked with fastq_utils v0.25.1. Quality assessment of reads was performed with FastQC v0.11.9 and reports were combined with MultiQC v1.12. rRNA percentages of reads were estimated with the 'hts_SeqScreener' program of htstream v1.3.3 screened against a fasta file of Mus-musculus rRNA sequences retrieved from NCBI on 09-May-2025.

OSD-93.study description: The aim of our research is to clarify the mechanisms generating heterogeneity in response to C-ion irradiation that arise from individual genetic variations in humans. In this study, we performed whole lung C-ion irradiation using three different strains of mice to examine whether strain-dependent differences in radiation effects occur in high-LET C-ion thoracic irradiation. Murine strain-variance was evaluated by histopathological examination of intra-alveolar hemorrhage that is likely to occur during the early phase after irradiation, and of lung fibrosis during the late phase, occurring more than three months after irradiation. We also performed microarray analysis to identify the key genes that are differentially regulated in different mouse strains after C-ion irradiation and to determine the mechanism of strain-dependent pulmonary damage after high-LET C-ion irradiation. Eight-week old female inbred C3H/He Slc, C57BL/6J Jms Slc and A/J Jms Slc mice (3 kinds of mice) were used. The whole thorax of three mice was locally irradiated at 10 Gy with C-ion beams, with a reference beam, 137Cs gamma-rays (2 kinds of beam). Three mice of each strain (3 mice) were sacrificed, and immediately dissected for lung extraction at 6 h (6h sample). Lungs for three mice of each strain without irradiation were extracted at the same time as control samples (control sample). Hybridization to microarrays (Whole Mouse Genome 4x44K OligoMicroarray Kit, single color, Cyamine 3-CTP) consisting of 44,000 total spots was conducted using an Agilent Gene Expression hybridization kit. The arrays from three independent replicates for each sample (3 arrays) were scanned on an Agilent dual-laser Microarray Scanner (all from Agilent Technologies) following the manufacturer's instructions. A total of 108 samples were analyzed. 3 replicate arrays x 3 mice x 3 strains x 2 timing for sampling x 2 kinds of beam.

study protocol description: Eight-week-old female inbred C3H/He Slc, C57BL/6J Jms Slc, and A/J Jms Slc mice were purchased from Japan SLC (Shizuoka, Japan). The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the National Institute of Radiological Sciences Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocol no. 07-2014-1).

Mice were anesthetized with pentobarbital (50 mg/kg body weight, intraperitoneal injection), and the whole thorax was locally irradiated with 10 Gy of 290 MeV/n C-ion beams generated by the Heavy Ion Medical Accelerator in Chiba (HIMAC) at the center of a 6-cm spread-out Bragg peak. The beams penetrated from the chest to the back, with the dose prescribed to the mid-plane of the mouse, which corresponded to a depth of 7 mm, assuming that the mouse had a homogeneous density equivalent to water. In control mice, the whole thorax was irradiated with 137Cs γ-rays in the same way. For the survival study, 10 mice were irradiated with 10 Gy or 12.5 Gy (C3H/He and A/J only) of C-ions, or with 10 Gy, 15 Gy, or 20 Gy of γ-rays, and they were observed over a period of 180 days after irradiation.
Cesium-137 produces gamma rays with an energy of 0.662 MeV and has a half-life of 30.1 years. Ionizing radiation energy values were added by GeneLab.

Both lungs were removed from three mice of each strain at 12 hours, 3 days, 5 days, 7 days, 56 days, 84 days, and 168 days after irradiation, and the wet weight was measured immediately. The lungs were completely dried in an incubator at 65°C for 24 hours for dry weight measurement. As an indication of lung edema, the ratio of lung weights (wet/dry) was determined.
For the other analyses, 10 mice of each strain were sacrificed at 6 hours, 14 days, 28 days, 56 days, 84 days, and 168 days after irradiation. Nonirradiated control samples were extracted at the same time. The right lobes of the lungs were placed in RNAlater (Ambion, Austin, TX) and stored at −20°C for gene expression analysis. The left lungs were fixed for 24 h in 10% neutralized formalin.

OSD-930.study description: Spaceflights significantly impacts astronaut health, causing muscle atrophy, bone loss, cardiovascular deconditioning and immune system dysregulation, especially during long missions. To explore molecular changes, we generated a single-cell RNA sequencing dataset, of 216 samples from 28 mouse organs and tissues under spaceflight and control conditions. Since spaceflight effects closely resemble aspects of aging, we included two age groups (3 and 8 months) to assess age-related influences. Our data revealed that spaceflight drives age-independent systemic changes, primarily affecting tissue remodeling and alterations in cytoskeleton, membrane and extracellular matrix (ECM), particularly in endothelial cells. In contrast, aging has a weaker impact, mainly altering immune regulation in an age-dependent manner. These findings suggest that cytoskeletal and ECM changes may contribute to immune Dysregulation.

CTX and CB were resuspended in 1 ml MACS buffer (0.5% BSA and 2 mM EDTA in PBS) with 1:500 RNase inhibitor and 1:10 myelin removal beads (Miltenyi Biotec 130-096-433). HIP and STR were resuspended in 500 ul MACS buffer with 1:500 RNase inhibitor and 1:10 myelin removal beads. All samples were incubated on ice for 10 minutes. The volume of CTX was adjusted to 2 ml with MACS buffer and the volumes of all other samples were adjusted to 1 ml, before loading CTX onto an LD column (Miltenyi Biotec 130-042-901), and CB, HIP, and STR onto LS columns (Miltenyi Biotec 130-042-401). Cells were then filtered into 35 um FACS tubes (Falcon 352235) and pelleted (400 x g, 5 minutes, Brake equals 5, 4C) before being resuspended in FACS buffer (1% FCS, 2 mM EDTA, and 25mM HEPES (pH 7.2-7.5) in PBS). Cells were then incubated on ice for 5 minutes in 1:60 Fc block (BD Pharmingen 553142), followed by 1:400 rabbit anti-mouse Tmem119 (Abcam ab210405) agitating for 10 minutes at 21C. After pelleting cells (400 x g, 5 minutes, Brake equals 5, 4C) and resuspending in FACS buffer, cells were stained with 1:300 CD45-PE-Cy7 (eBioscience 25-0451-82), 1:300 CD11b-BV421 (BioLegend 101236), and 1:300 Alexa 488 goat anti-rabbit (Invitrogen A11034) at 21C for 10 minutes. Cells were loaded in each channel with a target output of up to 5,000 cells per sample, though fewer cells were captured for small sample types. scRNA-seq libraries were constructed following the 10x Genomics protocol using the GemCode Single-Cell 3’ Gel Bead and Library v3 Kit. All reactions were performed in a Biorad C1000 Touch Thermal Cycler with a 96-Deep Well Reaction Module. Twelve cycles were used for cDNA amplification and sample index PCR. Amplified cDNA and final libraries were evaluated on a Fragment Analyzer using a High Sensitivity NGS Analysis Kit (Advanced Analytical). Library preparation was performed one organ type at a time, in sets of eight samples. Within each organ set, cDNA was normalized, and 13–20 PCR cycles were run depending on cDNA amount. The average fragment length of 10x cDNA libraries was quantified on a Fragment Analyzer (AATI) and by qPCR using the Kapa Library Quantification Kit for Illumina. Each library was diluted to 4 nM, and equal volumes were pooled for each sequencing run.

Sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform using 100-cycle run kits, with 28 bases for Read 1, 8 bases for Index 1, and 91 bases for Read 2 (Illumina 20012862). A PhiX control library was spiked in at 0.2–1%.

Quality assessment of reads was performed with FastQC v0.11.9 and reports were combined with MultiQC v1.12. rRNA percentages of reads were estimated with the 'hts_SeqScreener' program of htstream v1.3.3 screened against a fasta file of Mus-musculus rRNA sequences retrieved from NCBI on 09-May-2025.

OSD-933.acknowledgments: We thank Charles Chan for his assistance, who unfortunately passed away during the course of the project.
OSD-933.study description: Spaceflights significantly impacts astronaut health, causing muscle atrophy, bone loss, cardiovascular deconditioning and immune system dysregulation, especially during long missions. To explore molecular changes, we generated a single-cell RNA sequencing dataset, of 216 samples from 28 mouse organs and tissues under spaceflight and control conditions. Since spaceflight effects closely resemble aspects of aging, we included two age groups (3 and 8 months) to assess age-related influences. Our data revealed that spaceflight drives age-independent systemic changes, primarily affecting tissue remodeling and alterations in cytoskeleton, membrane and extracellular matrix (ECM), particularly in endothelial cells. In contrast, aging has a weaker impact, mainly altering immune regulation in an age-dependent manner. These findings suggest that cytoskeletal and ECM changes may contribute to immune Dysregulation.

study protocol description: Rodent Research Reference Mission 1 (RRR-1) / Rodent Research-8 (RR-8) consisted of 40 BALB/cAnNTac females (8 used for this study) termed Flight which were sent on 12/5/2018 to the International Space Station (ISS), and a control group of 40 mice remained on Earth, termed Habitat Ground Control (HC). Furthermore, two age groups were used, younger (∼3 months) and older (∼8 months). All mouse work was completed with approval of the NASA Flight Animal Care and Use Committee (Protocol FLT-18-116). Mice were received following landing at Scripps Research Institute (09-0004, for animal receipt upon landing) and transported to Stanford University IACUC (WYS1591). Flight mice were housed at double density on launch and again during the return to earth. HC mice were housed to match, as closely as possible, conditions experienced by Flight mice. This included double density housing in identical Mouse Habitat Units and Transporters as used by NASA during launch for Flight mice, and matched temperature, humidity, and carbon dioxide levels (elevated on the ISS compared to Earth) based on actual flight environmental monitoring. All mice were adapted to NASA Nutrient Food Bars, four weeks prior to launch, and bars were exchanged weekly. Mice had ad libitum access to both food and water. Mice had ad libitum access to both food and water. During the mission we encountered the following issues, altering the planned experimental design, or that must be considered upon interpretation of results. (1) Within 24h of the planned launch, mold was found on the food bars, affecting both Flight and HGC mice to an unknown degree. It is possible that the mice were able to eat around the mold. The late replacement of the food bars, now secured with double-sided tape instead of epoxy, caused the bars to free-float during launch and return. The bars of the HGC mice fell to the bottom of the cage. Although the Flight mice appeared healthy upon arrival to the ISS, this might have induced additional stress. Due to concerns about mold, as more was discovered aboard the ISS, the ISS Term mice were sacrificed after approximately 3 weeks of microgravity rather than the planned 8 weeks, and ground controls were sacrificed to match this new timeline.(2) Due to poor weather, the return of the Flight LAR mice was delayed and the mice spent 7 instead of the normal 2-3 days in double density housing. This housing is more confined (10 mice per cage side instead of the 5 in the normal habitat), video monitoring was not possible and food bars likely became unsecured and were free-floating. Conditions of the HGC mice were matched to these conditions, likely causing additional stress for both groups. Due to the weather, the Flight group likely experienced rough seas upon splashdown and shipping back to shore, which was not controlled for in the HGC group.

HC mice were shipped to Scripps Institute just prior to the return of the Flight mice so that all mice could be dissected together in matching conditions (+/- 1 day). The mice from the Flight group were returned alive to Earth on 1/14/2019 after 39.5 days on the ISS and collected 2-4 days after splashdown following functional assays at Scripps Research Institute. OSD-935.study description: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) play an important role in the regulation of skeletal muscle transcriptional processes, but their involvement in spaceflight- or inactivity-induced muscle atrophy remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we simulated the space environment by combining microgravity, irradiation and stress in a mouse model. Our results provide novel insights into the contribution of lncRNAs to muscle atrophy caused by the space exposome and has broader implications for understanding and combating muscle atrophy in clinical scenarios of prolonged inactivity.

study protocol description: All animal handling and experiments were carried out according to the ethical and welfare standards set forth by our institution's animal welfare committee at Medanex Clinic, Belgium, with approval from the local ethical committee (ethics approval number from Medanex Clinic: LA1100614). We used a HLU model that mimics all the stressors of the space exposome (microgravity, ionizing radiation and stress) to identify potential lncRNAs that play a role in space‐induced skeletal muscle alterations. Twenty 10‐week‐old male C57BL/6J mice were acquired from Janvier Labs SAS (Le Genest‐Saint‐Isle, France) and randomly assigned to one of two experimental groups: control (CONTROL) or spaceflight analogue (SPACE). The SPACE group was subjected to an acute dose of ionizing radiation, a chronic oral administration of a stress hormone and a HLU procedure. To compensate for the inability of the HLU mice to maintain body temperature through typical behaviours, all animals were housed at a temperature of 28 C, which approximates their thermoneutral zone. Mice underwent a 28‐day acclimatization period in solitary confinement within HLU cages maintained at 28C under a 12‐h light–dark cycle. During this acclimatization phase they were provided with a standard rodent diet and hydrogel as their drinking water, available ad libitum. In preparation for the subsequent 14-day HLU protocol, the mice were anaesthetized using isoflurane (5% for induction, 2% for maintenance via inhalation using a nose cone), and their tails were disinfected. Each SPACE mouse was secured to a HLU device at three points along the tail (proximal, mid and distal) using adhesive strapping (Tensoplast, Leuven, Belgium). The device was calibrated to maintain the mice in a head-down tilt position of approximately 30 degree, while still allowing them full access to the cage and the ability to rotate 360 degree. Throughout the HLU protocol daily assessments of food intake and body weight were recorded for all mice. The SPACE group had continuous ad libitum access to food and hydrogel, whereas the CONTROL group was pair fed, receiving an equivalent mass of food to that consumed by their matched SPACE counterparts. To induce chronic psychological stress SPACE mice were administered corticosterone (Sigma‐Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) at an estimated dose of 5 mg/kg/day, based on the method described by Dietrich et al. (2019). Corticosterone was delivered via hydrogel (as a replacement for their drinking water) for the entire 14‐day duration of the HLU procedure. Hydrogel was heated until melted, and corticosterone was added to a final concentration of 12.5 ug/g of hydrogel. The hydrogel was allowed to solidify and stored at 4C, and it was provided fresh daily to the mice in excess.

SPACE mice were irradiated on the seventh day of the HLU protocol at the Laboratory for Nuclear Calibrations (LNK) within the Belgian Nuclear Research Centre (SCK CEN). X‐rays of H‐250 beam quality, as specified by the ISO 4037 standard, were produced using a 320 kV tube (XStrahl, Walsall, UK) at LNK, with a current of 2.85 mA. The distance from the beam's focal point to the mice was 94.5 cm, and the X‐ray beam was directed vertically. Inherent filtration was performed using 3 mm of beryllium, supplemented by an additional 2.9 mm of aluminium and a dose area product monitor ionization chamber. The secondary standard air kerma measurements were traceable to international standards, adhering to the ISO 17025 accreditation of LNK. The cages housing the mice were consistently smaller than the diameter of the beam. Utilizing a dose rate of 7.965 Gy/h, the mice received an acute whole‐body dose of 1.000 plus or minus 0.033 Gy, which corresponds to the total accumulated dose equivalent for a round trip to Mars, based on a measured galactic cosmic ray (GCR) dose equivalent rate of 466 plus or minus 84 mSv for an outbound flight to Mars, as recorded by the Radiation Assessment Detector aboard the Mars Science Laboratory spacecraft (Guo et al., 2015). The irradiation protocol was executed while the mice remained suspended within their cages. CONTROL mice were transported to the irradiation facility but were not subjected to the radiation field (sham irradiation).

At the conclusion of the study, the mice were killed via an overdose of pentobarbital (125–250 mg/kg intraperitoneal), and their muscles were obtained and snap‐frozen in liquid nitrogen pre‐cooled isopentane.

One of the rear‐limb soleus muscle was used for RNA extraction. Briefly a bead beater device (BioSpec Products, Inc., Bartlesville, OK, USA) was used to homogenate the soleus muscle in TriZol (Invitrogen Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA, USA); then chloroform gradient separation and ethanol dilution were performed. Then the Direct‐zol RNA Miniprep Kit (Zymo Research, CA, USA) was used to purify the RNA following the instructions provided by the manufacturer.
RNA was depleted using Ribozero kit from Illumina stranded total RNA prep ligation with ribo zero library preparation protocol.
rRNA‐depleted libraries were pair‐end sequenced using NovaSeqXPlus platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA).

Fastq format was checked with fastq_utils v0.25.1. Quality assessment of reads was performed with FastQC v0.12.1 and reports were combined with MultiQC v1.26. rRNA percentages of reads were estimated with the 'hts_SeqScreener' program of htstream v1.3.3 screened against a fasta file of Mus-musculus rRNA sequences retrieved from NCBI on 09-May-2025.

Data were processed as described in GL-DPPD-7101-G (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/master/RNAseq/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7101_Versions/GL-DPPD-7101-G.md), using NF_RCP version 2.1.0 (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_RNASeq_Workflow/tree/NF_RCP_2.1.0). In short, raw fastq files were filtered using Trim Galore! (version 0.6.10) powered by Cutadapt (version 4.2). Trimmed fastq file quality was evaluated with FastQC (version 0.12.1), and MultiQC (version 1.26) was used to generate MultiQC reports. Mus Musculus STAR and RSEM references were built using STAR (version 2.7.11b) and RSEM (version 1.3.3), respectively, Ensembl release 112, genome assembly GRCm39 (Mus_musculus.GRCm39.dna.primary_assembly.fa) and the following gtf annotation file: Mus_musculus.GRCm39.112.gtf. Trimmed reads were aligned to the Mus Musculus STAR reference with STAR (version 2.7.11b) and alignment log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). Aligned reads were assessed for strandedness using RSeQC infer_experiment.py (version 5.0.4), gene body coverage using RSeQC geneBody_coverage.py (version 5.0.4), inner distance was assessed using RSeQC inner_distance.py (version 5.0.4), and distribution of RNA features using RSeQC read_distribution.py (version 5.0.4). Aligned reads from all samples were quantified using RSEM (version 1.3.3), with strandedness set to reverse and RSEM count log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). To create a set of rRNA-removed quantification data, Ensembl IDs mapping to ribosomal RNA (rRNA) were removed from the RSEM gene count data. Both the original set of RSEM quantification data and the rRNA-removed data were subject to differential gene expression analysis as follows. A runsheet was generated with dp_tools (version 1.3.8) and the runsheet and quantification data were imported to R (version 4.4.2) with tximport (version 1.34.0) and normalized with DESeq2 (version 1.46.0) median of ratios method. Normalized gene counts were subject to differential expression analysis. Differential expression analysis was performed in R (version 4.4.2) using DESeq2 (version 1.46.0); all groups were compared pairwise using the Wald test and the likelihood ratio test was used to generate the F statistic p-value. Gene annotations were assigned using the custom annotation tables generated in-house as detailed in GL-DPPD-7110-A (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/GL_RefAnnotTable-A_1.1.0/GeneLab_Reference_Annotations/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7110_Versions/GL-DPPD-7110-A/GL-DPPD-7110-A.md), with STRINGdb (version 2.16.4), PANTHER.db (version 1.0.12), and org.Mm.eg.db (version 3.19.1).

OSD-936.study description: Life on Earth has evolved in a form suitable for the gravitational force of 1 x g. Although the pivotal role of gravity in gene expression has been revealed by multi-omics approaches in space-flown samples and astronauts, the molecular details of how mammalian cells harness gravity have remained unclear. Here, we showed that mitochondria utilize gravity to activate protein synthesis within the organelle. Genome-wide ribosome profiling revealed reduced mitochondrial translation in mammalian cells and Caenorhabditis elegans under both microgravity at the International Space Station and simulated microgravity in a 3D-clinostat on the ground. We found that attenuation of cell adhesion through laminin-integrin interactions causes the phenotype. The downstream signaling pathway including FAK, RAC1, PAK1, BAD, and Bcl-2 family proteins in the cytosol, and mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis (mtFAS) pathway in the matrix maintain mitochondrial translation at high level. Mechanistically, a decreased level of mitochondrial malonyl-CoA, which is consumed by activated mtFAS, leads to a reduction in the malonylation of the translational machinery and an increase in the initiation and elongation of in organello translation. Consistent with the role of integrin as a mechanosensor, we observed a decrease in mitochondrial translation via the minimization of mechanical stress in mouse skeletal muscle. Our work provides mechanistic insights into how cells convert gravitational and mechanical forces into translation in an energy-producing organelle. This study hosts the human HEK293 cell datasets. The mouse datasets are available in OSD-955, and the C. elegans (nematode) datasets are available in OSD-956.

study protocol description: Spaceflight experiment: Disposable cultivation chambers (DCCs) were pretreated with laminin overnight as described below. Then, 5 x10^5 HEK293 cells were seeded in each DCC and incubated overnight. The medium was exchanged for CELLBANKER 1 plus (TaKaRa), and the cells were stored at -80 C. The frozen cells were then sent to the ISS by Cygnus NG-14 in October 2020. In the Japanese Experiment Module KIBO in the ISS, the samples were thawed, exchanged for DMEM, high glucose, GlutaMAX Supplement (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 10% FBS using a Pre-Fixation Kit-III (PFK-III, JAXA) and cultured under centrifugation at 1 x g in the Cell Biology Experiment Facility (CBEF) at 37 C with 5% CO2 and 80 +/-5% RH for 24 h. Subsequently, the cells were cultured under microgravity for 24 and 48 h, while the control cells were maintained at 1 × g.

Simulated microgravity ground-based experiment: To survey microgravity-mediated mitochondrial translation repression in the laboratory on the ground, we harnessed a clinostat that rotates the cell culture flask in three dimensions to reduce gravitational forces on the cells and simulate microgravity conditions. To test whether microgravity-mediated repression of mitochondrial translation is caused by reduced cell adhesion, we pretreated a cell culture flask with laminin, cultivated the cells under simulated microgravity, and then conducted ribosome profiling and RNASeq.

Spaceflight samples: For chemical fixation, the cell culture media were replaced with CELLBANKER 1 plus containing 100 ug/ml cycloheximide and 100 ug/ml chloramphenicol by PFK-III. The samples were subsequently stored in a Minus Eighty degree Celsius Laboratory Freezer for ISS (MELFI) at -95 C. The samples were returned to the ground by SpaceX CRS-22 (SpX-22) in July 2021 and shipped to the laboratory for ribosome profiling and RNA-seq. Simulated microgravity ground-based experiment: Cells in a DCC were washed with PBS and lysed with 500 ul of lysis buffer. After 25 U/ml TURBO DNase treatment (Thermo Fisher Scientific), the lysate was clarified by centrifugation at 20,000 x g for 10 min at 4 C.

The lysate was incubated with 25 U/ml TURBO DNase (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and clarified by centrifugation at 20,000 x g for 10 min at 4 C. For RNA-seq, total RNA was extracted from the same lysate used for ribosome profiling with TRIzol LS (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and a Direct-zol RNA Microprep Kit (Zymo Research). rRNA depletion was conducted with the Ribo-Zero Gold rRNA Removal Kit (Human/Mouse/Rat) (Illumina).

OSD-937.study description: Microgravity accelerates skeletal muscle degeneration, mimicking aspects of aging, yet its effects on muscle cell function remain underexplored. Using a muscle lab-on-chip model onboard the International Space Station (ISS), we examined 3D-bioengineered myobundles derived from young and older adult donors under microgravity. Electrical stimulation applied intermittently to the myobundles revealed reduced contraction magnitude in microgravity and decreased protein levels of myosin heavy chain 7, a main isoform in slow-twitch muscle fibers. Transcriptomic profiling revealed active myogenesis across ground and spaceflight samples, but younger electrically stimulated myobundles displayed enhanced mitochondrial-related gene expression in microgravity, while older and non-electrically stimulated myobundles were less responsive. Comparative analysis between young and older derived myobundles identified 86 muscle-specific age-associated genes altered in microgravity, linked to inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and cellular stress. These findings highlight a unique age-related molecular response in microgravity and underscores electrical stimulation as a potential countermeasure. These insights advance our understanding of muscle aging and degeneration in microgravity, guiding future therapeutic strategies.

study protocol description: Donor and muscle biopsy data analysis: Cells from the same lot of muscle biopsy cells used for our SpaceX CRS-21 mission (Parafati et al., 2023) were subsequently purified and seeded for the SpaceX CRS-25 mission and represented independent experiments. In brief, percutaneous biopsies were obtained from the middle region of the vastus lateralis using a Bergstrom needle (as previously described, Sparks et al., 2011), from five young, active male volunteers (mean 35 +/- 4) and five old, sedentary male volunteers (mean 70 +/- 4). Participants were considered active if they engaged in endurance exercise at least 3 days a week without extensive lay off over the previous 6 months. Participants were considered sedentary if they completed one or fewer structured exercise sessions a week. The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the institutional review board at AdventHealth, Orlando (IRBNet

554559). Myoblast purification: Harvested cells were purified with an immuno-magnetic sorting system (Miltenyi Biotec, Paris, France) using an anti-CD56/NCAM antibody as described (Giza et al., 2022). Purified myoblasts were plated in collagen-coated Petri dishes and cultured in skeletal muscle cell growth medium (PromoCell Cat

C-23060) supplemented with 0.1 mg/mL primosin to protect cultures from microbial contamination, 5% fetal bovine serum, and gentamicin at 37C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO2. At cell isolation, all human myoblasts were at passage 4 and expanded to passage 6. Passage numbers were matched for young- and old-derived donor cells. Myoblasts from different donors were pooled in a 1:1 ratio, and aliquots were cryopreserved. Enrichment was confirmed by comparing CD56− and CD56+ cell populations by fluorescence-activated cell sorting staining as described (Giza et al., 2022).

Donor-derived 3D myobundles were generated by seeding myoblasts in tissue-engineered constructs and launched to the ISS aboard the SpaceX CRS-25 commercial resupply mission. Cell seeding was performed at NASA’s Kennedy Space Station Processing Facility (SSPF) for flight and asynchronously at the University of Florida laboratory for the ground test. CD56+-enriched myoblasts were mixed in a collagen-Matrigel hydrogel and injected into the PDMS-based chips at a final cell density of 15 and 20 million cells/mL, for YA and OS-derived cell stocks, respectively, and allowed to polymerize at 37C for 60 min as previously described (Giza et al., 2022; Parafati et al., 2023). Differentiation followed a two-step process as previously described (Giza et al., 2022; Parafati et al., 2023, 2025). Sixteen tissue chips were integrated onto the CubeLab manifold on day 8 of growth, and media for flight was stored at 6C–8C in a gas-permeable bag. On day 14, 30 min of E-Stim of 3 V, 2 Hz, 2-ms pulse was applied sequentially to four YA and four OS tissue chips; the other eight chips were No E-Stim. Donor-derived 3D myobundles were maintained in the Space Tango CubeLab at 37C and 5%–6% CO2 for both the flight and ground payloads. The myobundles were cultured in maintenance medium that was changed every 6 h to maintain healthy muscle microtissues.

We performed transcript profiling of YA- and OS-derived myoblasts cultured for 2 and 21 days (including 12 days of spaceflight) and compared them with myoblasts grown on ground for the full 21 days by RNA-seq. Cultures in tissue chip devices were preserved with RNAlater (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and frozen at −20C to −30C.

Cells were lysed in the chip, and RNA isolation was performed using RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (QIAGEN) as previously described (Parafati et al., 2023). RNA concentration and quality were determined with Agilent TapeStation 2200 (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). 500 ng of total RNA was used for RNA sample preparation and processed in triplicate for a total of 30 samples.

Strand-specific RNA-seq libraries were generated using the NEBNext Ultra Directional RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NEB, USA) as previously described (Parafati et al., 2023). E7490). Then followed by RNA library construction with the NEBNext Ultra II Directional RNA Library Prep Kit (New England Biolabs, catalog

E7760) according to the manufacturer's user guide. Briefly, RNA was fragmented in NEBNext First Strand Synthesis Buffer via incubation at 94 C for the desired time. This step was followed by first-strand cDNA synthesis using reverse transcriptase and random hexamer primer. Synthesis of ds-cDNA was performed using the 2nd strand master mix provided in the kit, followed by end-repair and adaptor ligation. At this point, Illumina adaptors were ligated to the sample. Finally, each library (uniquely barcoded) was enriched by 12 cycles of amplification, and purified with Agencourt AMPure beads (Beckman Coulter, catalog
A63881). 15 barcoded libraries were sized on the TapeStation 4200 and quantified with the Qubit 2.0 Fluorometer.

Barcoded libraries were pooled equimolarly for sequencing simultaneously for Illumina NovaSeq X. Sequencing and bioinformatics were performed at the University of Florida Interdisciplinary Center for Biotechnology Research core facility.

OSD-939.study description: The current report assessed the effects of low-level proton irradiation in inbred adult male Fischer 344 and Lewis rats performing an analog of the human Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT), commonly utilized as an object risk assessment tool to quantify fatigue and sustained attention in laboratory, clinical, and operational settings. These strains were used to determine if genetic differences in dopaminergic function would impact radiation-induced deficits in sustained attention. Exposure to head-only proton irradiation (25 or 100 cGy) disrupted rPVT performance in a strain-specific manner, with 25 cGy-exposed Fischer 344 rats displaying the most severe deficits in sustained attention (i.e., decreased accuracy and increased premature responding); Lewis rats did not display behavioral deficits following radiation. Fischer 344 rats displayed greater tyrosine hydroxylase and dopamine transporter levels in the frontal cortex compared to the Lewis rats, even though radiation exposure increased both of these proteins in the Lewis rats only. Tyrosine hydroxylase was decreased in the parietal cortex of both rat strains following radiation exposure, regardless of proton dose. Strain-specific cytokine changes were also found in the frontal cortex, with the Lewis rats displaying increased levels of putative neurotrophic cytokines (e.g., CNTF). These data support the hypothesis that basal dopaminergic function impacts the severity of radiation-induced deficits in sustained attention. This study derives results from the Rodent Psychomotor Vigilance Test (rPVT) assay. Results from the Western Blot assays can be found in OSD-896 (frontal cortex) and OSD-897 (parietal cortex).
OSD-939.study funding agency: Supported by the National Space Biomedical Research Institute (NSBRI) through NASA cooperative agreement NCC 9-58, grants NBPF01604 (RDH), NBPF02802 (RDH), NBPF04201 (RDH), PF02602 (CMD), EO00010 (CMD), and NASA NNX15AC71G (CMD).
study protocol description: Subjects were 17 male Fischer 344 rats (Harlan Laboratories, Indianapolis, Indiana) and 20 Lewis rats, acquired at approximately 10–12 weeks of age. Rats were housed in individual plastic cages and maintained on a 12:12 h light/dark cycle (lights on at 6:00 AM) and at an ambient temperature of 23 degrees Celsius for the duration of the experiment. Rats were run in 30-min rPVT sessions during their light-on cycle at the same time each day in identically constructed operant chambers. Each rPVT chamber contained one nose-poke key, cue lights, a house light, and a food cup for delivery of food pellets. All chambers were contained in sound-attenuating enclosures equipped with an exhaust fan. The weights of the rats were maintained at 85–90 percent of each strain’s free-feeding weight by feeding measured amounts of rat chow each day (30 min after the experimental session, 5 days/week; at similar times on the weekends), in addition to the food that was earned during the behavioral test sessions. Water was freely available in the home cage. Laboratory animal care was according to Public Health Service (PHS) Policy on the Humane Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. This study was carried out in strict accordance with the recommendations in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of the National Institutes of Health. The protocol and all procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the Johns Hopkins University. Johns Hopkins also maintains accreditation of their program by the Association for the Assessment and Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care (AAALAC).

Rats were exported to Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) for radiation exposure 4–5 days prior to the scheduled exposure day. All animals were exposed on the same day, and then returned to Johns Hopkins for follow-up testing 4–5 days following exposure. While at BNL, rats were maintained under housing conditions similar to those at JHU, including the same light/dark cycle and were individually housed in plastic cages with a water bottle, wire top, and insulator top, that were filled with bedding and contained enrichment toys (i.e., Nyla bones). Rats also received ad lib access to water and food while at BNL. The control group was sham-irradiated, i.e., shipped to BNL, sedated and restrained for radiation exposure, but not actually exposed. The remaining rats were irradiated with 150 MeV/n protons generated at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) facility at BNL. Protons of this energy have a mean range in water of approximately 15.5 cm with an average LET of 0.4 keV/um. Target exposure levels were 25 and 100 cGy; actual delivered doses varied by no more than +/- 0.1 cGy relative to each target dose. Dose rates ranged from 30–71 cGy/min to achieve an even dose distribution across the collimated exposure field. Irradiation involved head-only exposures to minimize systemic responses to exposures that can confound morphological, neurochemical, and behavioral testing. For radiation exposures, rats received an intraperitoneal injection (2 ml/kg administered volume) of ketamine (90 mg/kg) and xylazine (5 mg/kg) and were subsequently placed in a ventilated polystyrene holder (2 rats/holder). Each body was shielded by a specially built trilaminar collimator exposure system consisting of Plexiglas, aluminum, and polyurethane; the body dose was less than 2 percent of the delivered dose.

Rats were run in 30-min rPVT sessions during their light-on cycle at the same time each day in identically constructed operant chambers. Each rPVT chamber contained one nose-poke key, cue lights, a house light, and a food cup for delivery of food pellets. All chambers were contained in sound-attenuating enclosures equipped with an exhaust fan. The weights of the rats were maintained at 85–90% of each strain’s free-feeding weight by feeding measured amounts of rat chow each day (30 min after the experimental session, 5 days/week; at similar times on the weekends), in addition to the food that was earned during the behavioral test sessions.

Before irradiation, rats were first trained to respond on a nose-poke key for food pellets on a fixed-ratio (FR) 1 schedule of reinforcement. Once this behavior was acquired, training on the rPVT procedure then began. The criterion for inclusion in the present study was that rats achieve at least 75% response accuracy and less than a 25% false alarm rate, resulting in a d’ index of 1.35, for four out of the five daily test sessions during each of the two weeks prior to radiation. Most rats achieved this criterion more than two weeks prior to radiation, and the average pre-exposure d’ index achieved for F344 and LEW rats was 1.9 and 2.0, respectively (accuracy of 78.1% and false alarm rate of 15.9% for F344; accuracy of 79.6% and false alarm rate of 15.9% for LEW). Thus all rats included in the study acquired and maintained stable rPVT performances prior to the exposure.

Rats were run in 30-min rPVT sessions during their light-on cycle at the same time each day in identically constructed operant chambers. Each rPVT chamber contained one nose-poke key, cue lights, a house light, and a food cup for delivery of food pellets. Post-irradiation rPVT performances were monitored for 34 weeks following exposure. Sessions began with the onset of the house light. After a variable delay of 3–10 sec the light behind the nose-poke key was illuminated. A correct response was defined as a response on the nose poke key within 1.5 sec after the light onset (i.e., 1.5-sec limited hold, LH) and was reinforced with a pellet. A response prior to the light onset (premature response) was not reinforced and punished with an 8 sec time out, while a response after the 1.5-sec interval had elapsed (miss) was not reinforced. The delay period for the next trial began after a 3-sec inter-trial interval, timed either after the response or the end of the 1.5-sec LH, whichever occurred first.

For the rPVT procedure, experimental contingencies were controlled by MedPC behavioral control programs running on PCs; the programs recorded all data on a trial-by-trial basis to provide for a wide range of subsequent analyses. Data collected were the numbers of correct responses as defined above, premature responses (responses that occurred prior to the light onset), misses (number of 1.5-sec light-on intervals during which no response occurred), and lapses in responding (misses plus responses greater than twice the rat’s mean response latency). Summary measures were expressed as percentages, as follows: accuracy equals correct responses / (corrects plus premature responses plus misses); premature responding equals number of premature responses / (corrects plus premature responses plus misses); lapse rate equals (misses plus lapses) / (corrects plus premature responses plus misses). In the human literature on PVT performance, lapses are considered an important indicator of inattention and/or fatigue and are typically defined as responses with latencies greater than 500 msec, or roughly twice the average latency for humans performing the 10-min version of the test. For rodents, average latency can vary considerably from subject to subject, and so the definition adopted here was based on each rat’s individual mean latency measure (described in https://doi.org/10.1667/RR13359.1). Premature responding was broken down further by calculating a false alarm (FA) rate for those premature responses occurring within the 3–10 second delay period (i.e., FA rate equals premature responses within the 3–10 sec delay interval / (corrects plus premature responses within the 3–10 sec delay interval plus misses). The addition of a false alarm measure allowed for the calculation of a d’ index of signal discriminability in which percent correct (PC) scores and false alarm (FA) rates are converted into z scores, and subtracted (d’ equals z(PC)-z(FA). This performance measure is important for calculating a d prime (d’) measure of discriminability that can be compared across the different strains. Finally, response latencies to the light onset were recorded in milliseconds, and summarized by calculating both the median and mean reaction times.

To enable maximal data reuse (for machine-readable approaches), the submitted version of this dataset was subsequently transformed and edited to be aligned with a reusable template, which was created through feedback provided by subject matter experts in the ALSDA Analysis Working Group. This transformed reusable version is structured so all results are standardized into specific rows (source/subject) and columns (measures). This enables all assay results to be identically structured for efficient data mining. Please refer to the study-level data dictionary file for a complete list of column header names and descriptions.

OSD-940.study description: Cellular and molecular dynamics of human cells are constantly affected by gravity. study protocol description:
Clinostat setup: The 3D clinostat was developed and validated in the previous research. The is adept at providing simulated microgravity (taSMG) conditions at levels less than 10^-3G. To contextualize, 1G represents the standard acceleration due to Earth’s gravity, quantified as 9.806 m/s2. In the operational context of the 3D clinostat, certain forces such as Coriolis, radial, and frictional forces were deemed negligible. This assessment is based on the relatively minimal angular velocities achieved by the two axes of the clinostat, specifically, the inner frame rotating at 0.683 revolutions per minute (rpm), which is equivalent to approximately 4.098 degrees per second and the outer frame at 0.913 rpm, which is equivalent to approximately 5.478 degrees per second. These rotations ensure that the gravitational vector is continuously randomized, effectively simulating a microgravity environment. Importantly, maintaining these specified angular velocities is crucial in the 3D clinostat’s functionality, as it
ensures the avoidance of repetitive gravitational vector patterns. The efficacy of these operational parameters in achieving the desired simulated microgravity has been convincingly demonstrated in the aforementioned research.

Colorectal cancer organoid culture: Each organoid line was derived from four independent patient samples, with each organoid line representing one biological replicate. These organoid lines were cultured separately to maintain their unique biological
characteristics. The culture medium for human colorectal cancer (CRC) organoids was renewed every five days. Imaging of CRC organoids was taken during early passages (p1-p5). For passaging, the basement membrane extract (BME) dome was disrupted by mechanical pipetting using TrypLE Express solution (GIBCO, Catalog

12604-021), followed by the collection of organoids in a 15 mL conical tube. This BME dome was then subjected to vigorous pipetting for mechanical dissociation. The tube, containing the organoid-BME mixture, was incubated at 37 C for approximately 5–10 min. Subsequently, the organoids were centrifuged at 1,000 rpm for 3 min, and the supernatant was carefully removed. After the removal of BME, the resultant cell pellet was reconstituted in fresh BME and transferred into a T-25 flask. This flask was then incubated at 37 C for 10 min. Following the solidification of BME, 5 mL of culture medium was added to overlay the BME dome, and the cells were incubated in a 37 C incubator with 5% CO2. The setting of clinostat was previously described. For the experiments conducted under simulated microgravity, each organoid line (from the four patient-derived samples) was subjected to the clinostat conditions in triplicate. This resulted in three biological replicates per organoid line under both simulated microgravity and normal gravity conditions.
Following a 14-day culture period in the clinostat, we extracted total mRNA from the organoids.
Total RNA was isolated from cell lysate using TRIzol (Qiagen) and Qiagen RNeasy kit (Qiagen, Cat
74104). RNA sequencing was conducted on each of the four organoid lines, with one biological replicates per condition (simulated microgravity and normal gravity).
RNA libraries for RNA-seq were prepared using TruSeq Stranded mRNA LT Sample Prep Kit using manufacturer's protocols.
Paired end sequencing reads of cDNA libraries (101 bp) generated from a NovaSeq6000 instrument were verified its sequence quality with FastQC v 0.11.7.

Fastq format was checked with fastq_utils v0.25.1. Quality assessment of reads was performed with FastQC v0.12.1 and reports were combined with MultiQC v1.26. rRNA percentages of reads were estimated with the 'hts_SeqScreener' program of htstream v1.3.3 screened against a fasta file of H-sapiens rRNA sequences retrieved from NCBI on 09-May-2025.

Data were processed as described in GL-DPPD-7101-G (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/master/RNAseq/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7101_Versions/GL-DPPD-7101-G.md), using NF_RCP version 2.1.0 (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_RNASeq_Workflow/tree/NF_RCP_2.1.0). In short, raw fastq files were filtered using Trim Galore! (version 0.6.10) powered by Cutadapt (version 4.2). Trimmed fastq file quality was evaluated with FastQC (version 0.12.1), and MultiQC (version 1.26) was used to generate MultiQC reports. Homo Sapiens STAR and RSEM references were built using STAR (version 2.7.11b) and RSEM (version 1.3.3), respectively, Ensembl release 112, genome assembly GRCh38 (Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.dna.primary_assembly.fa) and the following gtf annotation file: Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.112.gtf. Trimmed reads were aligned to the Homo Sapiens STAR reference with STAR (version 2.7.11b) and alignment log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). Aligned reads were assessed for strandedness using RSeQC infer_experiment.py (version 5.0.4), gene body coverage using RSeQC geneBody_coverage.py (version 5.0.4), inner distance was assessed using RSeQC inner_distance.py (version 5.0.4), and distribution of RNA features using RSeQC read_distribution.py (version 5.0.4). Aligned reads from all samples were quantified using RSEM (version 1.3.3), with strandedness set to reverse and RSEM count log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). To create a set of rRNA-removed quantification data, Ensembl IDs mapping to ribosomal RNA (rRNA) were removed from the RSEM gene count data. Both the original set of RSEM quantification data and the rRNA-removed data were subject to differential gene expression analysis as follows. A runsheet was generated with dp_tools (version 1.3.8) and the runsheet and quantification data were imported to R (version 4.4.2) with tximport (version 1.34.0) and normalized with DESeq2 (version 1.46.0) median of ratios method. Normalized gene counts were subject to differential expression analysis. Differential expression analysis was performed in R (version 4.4.2) using DESeq2 (version 1.46.0); all groups were compared pairwise using the Wald test and the likelihood ratio test was used to generate the F statistic p-value. Gene annotations were assigned using the custom annotation tables generated in-house as detailed in GL-DPPD-7110-A (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/GL_RefAnnotTable-A_1.1.0/GeneLab_Reference_Annotations/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7110_Versions/GL-DPPD-7110-A/GL-DPPD-7110-A.md), with STRINGdb (version 2.16.4), PANTHER.db (version 1.0.12), and org.Hs.eg.db (version 3.19.1).

study protocol description: Twenty-two men (32.3 +/- 6.2 years, 178.3 +/- 6.3 cm, 78.4 +/- 10.1 kg) out of 26 subjects who had completed the intervention and had muscle biopsies to perform genomic analysis were included in this study. Procedures were approved by the institutional review boards at the NASA Johnson Space Center and the University of Texas Medical Branch (UTMB). All subjects provided written informed consent for participation in the bed rest protocols. The study protocol was implemented at the UTMB Institute for Translational Sciences – Clinical Research Center in a dedicated hospital unit referred to as the NASA Flight Analogs Research Unit. A complete description of the subject recruitment, screening and selection criteria can be found in Cromwell et al.. Following consent procedures, subjects were randomized to one of three groups: 1) control; no exercise, bed rest only (CON; n equals 7), 2) bed rest + aerobic and resistance exercise using traditional exercise equipment (EX; n equals 7), and 3) bed rest + aerobic and resistance exercise using a single flywheel device (FLY; n equals 8).

Bed Rest and Exercise Training: Baseline data collection was completed with subjects living at the research unit. Subjects were confined to bed rest for 70 days in a 6-degree head-down tilt position and monitored 24 hours daily. Subjects remained at the research facility during the post bed rest data collection. The head-down tilt position was maintained throughout the study except during meals and with aerobic and resistance exercise training (supine or prone horizontal position) and rowing (upright seated position). Exercise was prescribed using the SPRINT protocol consisting of aerobic exercise 6 days per week, 15–35 min/session, and resistance exercise 3 days per week, 35–60 min/session, described in detail previously. In brief, subjects completed alternating days of high-intensity interval (near max intensity) and continuous aerobic training (75% VO2peak) on a supine cycle ergometer and zero-gravity locomotion simulator vertical treadmill respectively. To avoid the known incompatibilities of resistance and aerobic training, these activities occurred concurrently only on the lower intensity continuous aerobic training days. Additionally, training sessions were separated by at least 4 hours. Subjects completed three sets of six to twelve repetitions of four supine lifts: 1) squat, 2) leg press, 3) unilateral leg curl, and 4) heel raise. In the EX group, subjects performed aerobic exercise on a vertical treadmill (high-intensity interval aerobic training) or a supine electronic cycle ergometer (continuous aerobic exercise; Lode B.V., Groningen, the Netherlands). Resistance exercise was conducted on the horizontal leg press (Quantum Fitness, Stafford, TX) and prone leg curl machines (Cybex International, Medway, MA). In the FLY group, subjects completed both aerobic (seated rowing) and resistance exercise (supine) on a single custom-built flywheel device. The squat exercise could not be performed on the flywheel; therefore to maintain consistent exercise volume, the number of sets was increased from three to four for the following three exercises: 1) heel raise, 2) hamstring curl, and 3) leg press. Due to the nature of the flywheel device, each repetition was completed with maximum exertion. For further details on the 6-degree head-down tilt and specialized exercise equipment, please refer to Cromwell (2018).

Muscle biopsies of the vastus lateralis were performed in the basal state in the morning one day before and on day 64 of the bed rest study. No testing or training was conducted for around 20 hours before the biopsy.

Total RNA was extracted from the VL muscle using TRIzol (Gibco BRL Life Technologies, Rockville, MD) for both gene and microRNA expression analysis. For gene expression only, RNA was purified using the Qiagen-RNeasy Mini Kit. Resuspension of RNA pellets was done in diethyl pyrocarbonate-treated water. Assessment of RNA integrity was performed prior to beginning analytical processing using an Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100 (Agilent Technologies, Inc., Palo Alto, CA, USA). Only samples with an RNA integrity number (RIN) greater than or equals to 9.1 were analyzed.

A template for double-stranded cDNA synthesis was created using 200 ng total RNA and a portion of this was used to generate biotin-tagged cRNA from an in vitro transcription reaction (IVT), using an Agilent Low Input Quick Amp Labeling Kit that generates fluorescent cRNA. The method uses T7 RNA Polymerase, which amplifies the target material and incorporates Cyanine 3_ATP. Amplification is typically 100-fold from total RNA to cRNA.

The SurePrint G3 Human Gene Expression v3 8×60K Microarray Chip arrays were hybridized overnight at 65C, washed and then scanned using Agilent’s SureScan Scanner (Agilent Technologies, Palo Alto, CA).
Data was collected using Agilent’s Feature Extraction software version 10.7 (Agilent Technologies, Palo Alto, CA).

study protocol description: Sampling materials consisted of

sterile polyester wipes (TX3211 Texwipe) moistened with 10ml of sterile molecular grade water and stored in 50ml conical bottom tubes (BD Falcon). Wipes were removed from tubes and handled with sterile gloves during sampling. Sampling consisted of folding wipes into quarters, wiping an area of approximately 1m^2 unidirectionally, folding to a new quarter of a wipe, wiping the same area in a different direction, and repeating for a total of 3 directions. Wipes were rolled up, placed back in the tubes, and transported to the lab for processing.

Sampling materials (sterile TX3211 (Texwipe) wipes moistened with molecular grade water) were extracted with PBS+Tween80, concentrated with Amicon concentrators, and extracted with Qiagen UCP pathogen miniprep kit. Zymo MMC samples were diluted from the D6306 Microbial Community DNA Standard. DNA was amplified with the Repli-G Midi Kit (Qiagen). Samples Zymo_MMC_Even_125pg, D1S5, D1S8, D1S10, D2S9, and NTC_1 were stopped at 12 hours of MDA reaction. Samples D2S2, D2S6, D2S7, D2S8, D2S10 ran Sampling materials (sterile TX3211 (Texwipe) wipes moistened with molecular grade water) were extracted with PBS+Tween80, concentrated with Amicon concentrators, and extracted with Qiagen UCP pathogen miniprep kit. Zymo MMC samples were diluted from the D6306 Microbial Community DNA Standard. DNA was amplified with the Repli-G Midi Kit (Qiagen). Samples Zymo_MMC_Even_125pg, D1S5, D1S8, D1S10, D2S9, and NTC_1 were stopped at 12 hours of MDA reaction. Samples D2S2, D2S6, D2S7, D2S8, D2S10 ran overnight (approximately 12 hours). All other samples were stopped at 2 hours of MDA reaction. MDA product was treated with T7 Endonuclease (New England Biolabs) and cleaned with the magnetic AXP beads from the Nanopore Rapid PCR Barcoding Kit 24 V14.

DNA libraries were prepared with the Nanopore Rapid PCR Barcoding Kit 24 V14 (Oxford Nanopore Technologies, Oxford, UK) following the manufacturer's protocol, using 14 PCR cycles. Library quality was assayed for each sample using the High Sensitivity D1000 DNA ScreenTape (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA) following the manufacturer's protocol. Sample libraries were pooled into 3 multiplex libraries. Multiplex library 1 contained samples Zymo_MMC_Even_125pg, D1S5, D1S8, D1S10, D2S9, and NTC_1. Multiplex library 2 contained samples Zymo_MMC_Even_2, D1S1, D2S1, and NTC_2. Multiplex library 3 contained all other samples. Sample libraries with Qubit values above the detection limit were pooled with eqimolar concentration and if sample libraries were below the Qubit detection limit, the maximum volume (49uL) was used. Multiplex library concentration was measured with Qubit 1x dsDNA HS assay (ThermoFisher Scientific). Final library loaded was 50 fmol.
DNA libraries were sequenced with the PromethION 2 Solo system and Minknow Software v25.03.9. 87 hour sequencing time; all other settings default

Fastq files were generated from the PromethION 2 Solo software using Dorado v7.8.3. Fastq files for each barcode were concatenated into one fastq file per barcode, then quality was assessed with Nanoplot v1.44.1 and reports were summarized with MultiQC v1.27.1.

Note: The samples in this dataset were sequenced in 3 separate sequencing runs. The data was processed in parallel for all three sequencing runs and then combined in the QC reports and visualizations.
Quality assessment: Quality assessment of filtered, trimmed, blanks-removed (decontaminated) and human-removed reads was performed with Nanoplot v1.44.1 and reports were combined with MultiQC v1.27.1.
Pre-processing: Raw concatenated reads were filtered by quality (Phred quality greater than or equal to 8) and length (greater than or equal to 200bp) using filtlong v0.2.1. Adapters were then removed from the filtered reads using porechop v0.2.4. Quality controlled blank / negative control sample reads were assembled using Flye v2.9.5. Contaminant (blank) reads were removed from the samples by mapping quality filtered/trimmed reads to the assembled blank contigs using minimap2 v2.28. Then, unmapped/decontaminated reads were identified and output to decontaminated fastq files using samtools v1.20. After contaminant removal, human reads were removed using kraken2 v2.1.4 against a human genome reference database that was constructed from NCBI's RefSeq (GCF_000001405.39) GRCh38.p13. The database was constructed by running the kraken build command with the following parameter set --no-masking, --kmer-length 35 and --minimizer-length 31.
Read-based processing: Taxonomy assignment of decontaminated/human-removed reads was performed with Kraken2 v2.1.4 and Kaiju v1.10.1. The resulting assignments were visualized as krona plots using krona v2.8.1.
Assembly-based analysis: The decontaminated/human-removed reads were assembled with Flye v2.9.5 then polished using medaka v2.0.1. Genes were called with prodigal v2.6.3. Taxonomic classification of genes and contigs was performed with CAT v5.2.3. Functional annotation was done with KOFamScan v1.3.0. Reads were mapped to assembles with minimap2 v2.28, and coverage information was extracted for both reads and contigs with samtools v1.20 and bbmap v38.86. Binning of contigs was performed with metabat2 v2.15. Bins were summarized with bit v1.8.53 and estimates of bin quality were generated with checkm v1.1.3. High-quality bins (greater than 90% est. completeness and less than 10% est. redundancy) were taxonomically classified with gtdb-tk v2.4.0 as MAGs (Metagenome-assembled genomes). Assemblies were created for each sample, but no gene calls were identified for NTC_3. Bins were recovered for only 5 samples. No MAGs were recovered.
Feature table decontamination and visualizations: All graphical displays were conducted using R v4.5.1. Bar plots and heatmaps were generated using R packages ggplot2 v3.5.1 and pheatmap v1.0.13, respectively. Taxonomy and function annotation tables from both read- and assembly-based processing steps were decontaminated with decontam v1.24.0, an R package designed to statistically identify contaminant features in a feature table. **

Note: Some reports contain output information for multiple columns. As such they are linked multiple times in the assay table under each relevant column but are only located under one of the shared directories.

Sampling materials (sterile TX3211 (Texwipe) wipes moistened with molecular grade water) were extracted with PBS+Tween80, concentrated with Amicon concentrators, and extracted with Qiagen UCP pathogen miniprep kit.

Samples were prepared using the Illumina Nextera XT DNA Library Preparation kit following the manufacturer's protocol. An equal volume of each sample library was used to create a library pool, which was sequenced on a MiSeq i100+ instrument at 2x159 cycles. The sample pool was balanced based on the results to create the final sample pool. The final loading concentration was 140 pmol.

Sequencing of the final DNA library pool was performed at DNA Services Facility at the Roy J. Carver Biotechnology Center at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. The final pool was sequenced on 1 lane of a XX flow cell on a NovaSeq X sequencer with the following set-up: R1:150, R2:150, i7:10, i5:10. BCL files were demultiplexed in BaseSpace using Dragen BCL-Convert 4.3.16.
Fastq file quality was assessed with FastQC v0.12.1 and reports were summarized with MultiQC v1.19. See GeneLab data processing protocol for information regarding HR-removal.

Pre-processing: Quality assessment of reads was performed with FastQC v0.12.1 and reports were combined with MultiQC v1.19. Quality-trimming and filtering was performed with fastp v0.24.0. Quality controlled blank/negative control sample reads were assembled using SPAdes v4.1.0. Contaminant (blank) reads were removed from the samples by mapping quality filtered/trimmed reads to the assembled blank contigs using Bowtie2 v2.4.1. The database was constructed by running the kraken build command with the following parameter set --no-masking, --kmer-length 35 and --minimizer-length 31.
Read-based processing: Taxonomy assignment of decontaminated/human-removed reads was performed with three tools: Kraken v2.1.6, Kaiju v1.10.1, and MetaPhlAn v4.1.0. The resulting assignments from each tool were visualized as krona plots using krona v2.8.1.

Taxonomy and function annotation tables from both read- and assembly-based processing steps were decontaminated with decontam v1.24.0, an R package designed to statistically identify contaminant features in a feature table.

Only samples with an RNA integrity number (RIN) greater than or equals to 9.1 were analyzed.

One hundred ng of total RNA from each sample was labeled with the fluorescent dye Cyanine 3-pCp (Cy3) using the microRNA Labeling Reagent and Hybridization Kit (Agilent Technologies, Palo Alto, CA) following the manufacturer’s protocol.
Cy3-labeled RNA was hybridized to Agilent Human microRNA Version 2 Microarray from each sample.

The hybridized array was then washed and scanned according to Agilent specifications and data was extracted from the scanned image using Feature Extraction software version 10.7 (Agilent Technologies, Palo Alto, CA).

OSD-949.study description: The 5' adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is an important skeletal muscle regulator implicated as a possible therapeutic target to ameliorate the local undesired deconditioning of disuse atrophy. However, the muscle-specific role of AMPK in regulating muscle function, fibrosis, and transcriptional reprogramming during physical disuse is unknown. The purpose of this study was to determine how the absence of both catalytic subunits of AMPK in skeletal muscle influences muscle force production, collagen deposition, and the transcriptional landscape. We generated skeletal muscle-specific tamoxifen-inducible AMPKa1/a2 knockout mice that underwent 14 days of hindlimb unloading (HU) or remained ambulatory for 14 days (AMB). We found that AMPKa-/- during ambulatory conditions altered body weight and myofiber size, decreased muscle function, depleted glycogen stores and TBC1 domain family member 1 (TBC1D1) phosphorylation, increased collagen deposition, and altered transcriptional pathways. Primarily, pathways related to cellular senescence and mitochondrial biogenesis and function were influenced by the absence of AMPKa. The effects of AMPKa-/- persisted, but were not worsened, following hindlimb unloading. Together, we report that AMPKa is necessary to maintain skeletal muscle quality.

study protocol description: All experimental procedures were approved by an independent review committee and conducted in accordance with the guidelines set by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at the University of Utah. Female (n equals 23) and male (n equals 22) C57BL/6J mice aged 3 or 4 mo were housed with ad libitum access to standard chow (Envigo 2920X) and water while maintained on a 12-h light/dark cycle with the lights on at 6:00 AM (zeitgeber time; ZT0) and off at 6:00 PM (ZT12). AMPKalpha1/alpha2 double-floxed mice were generated as described by Nakada et al. and crossed with human-alpha skeletal actin MerCreMer (HSA-MCM) mice to generate tamoxifen-inducible skeletal muscle-specific AMPKalpha1/alpha2 double knockout mice. In brief, exon 3 of Ampkalpha1 and exon 2 of the Ampkalpha1 gene were flanked with loci of X-over P1 (LoxP) sites, and in response to Cre recombinase (Cre) activation under the control of the human-alpha skeletal actin (ACTA1) promoter, they were excised and recombined. AMPKalpha1/alpha2 double-floxed mice (AMPKalphafl/fl) lacking HSA-MCM were used as controls and compared with littermate heterozygous Cre-containing double knockout mice (AMPKalpha−/−). AMPKa phosphorylation, AMPKalpha total protein, and downstream acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) phosphorylation were reduced only in skeletal, but not cardiac, muscle, validating efficient and specific knockout in skeletal muscle. Mice were injected daily with 2 mg/day of tamoxifen adjusted for their body weight for 5 consecutive days. Fourteen days after the last tamoxifen injection, mice either remained ambulatory (AMB; n equals 8 F, 9 M) or were hindlimb unloaded (HU; n equals 12 F, 10 M) for 14 days. Hindlimb unloading was conducted as we have previously described. In brief, mice underwent a modified Morey-Holton hindlimb unloading design and were housed 2/cage with mice of the same sex and genotype. Body weight, water, and food intake were monitored to confirm no excessive weight loss due to malnutrition or dehydration.

Following either 14 days of AMB or HU, mice were fasted for 3 or 4 h beginning at 7:00 AM (ZT1) until 10:00 or 11:00 AM (ZT3 or 4) and soleus, gastrocnemius, plantaris, tibialis anterior (TA), and extensor digitorum longus (EDL) hindlimb muscles were collected under isoflurane anesthetization and snap frozen in liquid nitrogen for subsequent analysis or used fresh for ex vivo isometric force production measurements.

Total RNA was isolated from soleus muscle by homogenizing 1 mg of tissue in Qiazol Lysis Reagent (Qiagen, Cat. No. 79306) with a TissueLyser II (Qiagen) and processed with the Zymo Research Direct-zol RNA Microprep Kit (Cat. No. R2061) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Extracted RNA was suspended in nuclease-free water.
Libraries were prepared with Illumina Stranded Total RNA Library Prep NEB Ultra II directional RNA library prep with rRNA depletion.
RNA was sequenced using Illumina NovaSeq S4 Reagent Kit v1.5 151 x 151 bp Sequencing (25 M read pairs per sequencing lane).

Fastq format was checked with fastq_utils v0.25.1. Quality assessment of reads was performed with FastQC v0.12.1 and reports were combined with MultiQC v1.26. rRNA percentages of reads were estimated with the 'hts_SeqScreener' program of htstream v1.3.3 screened against a fasta file of Mus-musculus rRNA sequences retrieved from NCBI on 09-May-2025.

Data were processed as described in GL-DPPD-7101-G (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/master/RNAseq/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7101_Versions/GL-DPPD-7101-G.md), using NF_RCP version 2.1.0 (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_RNASeq_Workflow/tree/NF_RCP_2.1.0). In short, raw fastq files were filtered using Trim Galore! (version 0.6.10) powered by Cutadapt (version 4.2). Trimmed fastq file quality was evaluated with FastQC (version 0.12.1), and MultiQC (version 1.26) was used to generate MultiQC reports. Mus Musculus STAR and RSEM references were built using STAR (version 2.7.11b) and RSEM (version 1.3.3), respectively, Ensembl release 112, genome assembly GRCm39 (Mus_musculus.GRCm39.dna.primary_assembly.fa) and the following gtf annotation file: Mus_musculus.GRCm39.112.gtf. Trimmed reads were aligned to the Mus Musculus STAR reference with STAR (version 2.7.11b) and alignment log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). Aligned reads were assessed for strandedness using RSeQC infer_experiment.py (version 5.0.4), gene body coverage using RSeQC geneBody_coverage.py (version 5.0.4), inner distance was assessed using RSeQC inner_distance.py (version 5.0.4), and distribution of RNA features using RSeQC read_distribution.py (version 5.0.4). Aligned reads from all samples were quantified using RSEM (version 1.3.3), with strandedness set to reverse and RSEM count log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). To create a set of rRNA-removed quantification data, Ensembl IDs mapping to ribosomal RNA (rRNA) were removed from the RSEM gene count data. Both the original set of RSEM quantification data and the rRNA-removed data were subject to differential gene expression analysis as follows. A runsheet was generated with dp_tools (version 1.3.8) and the runsheet and quantification data were imported to R (version 4.4.2) with tximport (version 1.34.0) and normalized with DESeq2 (version 1.46.0) median of ratios method. Normalized gene counts were subject to differential expression analysis. Differential expression analysis was performed in R (version 4.4.2) using DESeq2 (version 1.46.0); all groups were compared pairwise using the Wald test and the likelihood ratio test was used to generate the F statistic p-value. Gene annotations were assigned using the custom annotation tables generated in-house as detailed in GL-DPPD-7110-A (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/GL_RefAnnotTable-A_1.1.0/GeneLab_Reference_Annotations/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7110_Versions/GL-DPPD-7110-A/GL-DPPD-7110-A.md), with STRINGdb (version 2.16.4), PANTHER.db (version 1.0.12), and org.Mm.eg.db (version 3.19.1).

OSD-95.study description: Bacterial behavior has been observed to change during spaceflight. Higher final cell counts, enhanced biofilm formation, increased virulence, and reduced susceptibility to antibiotics have been reported to occur for cells cultured in space . Most of these phenomena are theorized as being an indirect effect of an altered extracellular environment, where the carbon source uptake is inhibited and excreted acidic byproducts buildup around the cell due to the lack of gravity-driven transport forces. However, to date neither spaceflight results, ground-based studies, physical measurement techniques nor computational approaches have provided sufficient evidence needed to confirm this model. Gene expression data from the Antibiotic Effectiveness in Space (AES-1) experiment, however, have now allowed us to look into the biomolecular processes behind these observations and showed a systematic activation of glucose starvation and acid resistance genes. These results corroborate the reduced mass transport model proposed to govern bacterial responses to spaceflight. Furthermore, the gene expression data suggests that metabolism was stimulated in space, which could play a role in causing the observed increase in bacterial cell concentrations in microgravity. Similarly, the decrease in extracellular pH may also be involved with the reported increase in virulence in space.
